I'm pulling up the actual wording of Prop 5 from the Secretary of State, starting with the amendment to Section 15 of Article II. The recall clause says that if a majority votes to recall, the officer is removed, and the candidate with a plurality takes over, but the officer can't run and the office stays vacant.

I'm checking the rest of the Section 15(c) wording: the vacancy gets filled under the Constitution and statute, but the officer who was recalled can't be appointed to fill it.

I'm working through the text of the amendment and trying to separate the struck language from the new insertions, since the extraction doesn't mark which is which. The open question is whether the ban on the officer running for the office is being kept or removed.

The sources I'm citing all describe the current ban as one the constitution imposes on the recalled officer running in the replacement election, so the struck language is probably the "may not be a candidate" sentence. That would fit the new insertion barring only appointment, not candidacy.

I'm checking how the Section 16(d) reference fits in: the text seems to be striking the ban on a candidacy for a legislative vacancy filled by special election, and I'm not sure yet whether that clause is being kept or removed.

I'm weighing whether the recall text bars candidacy for a special election under Article VI, Section 16(d), and what that clause would mean for the replacement candidate. It reads oddly, so I'm checking whether the prohibition covers running in the legislative special election for the same seat.

I'm going to check whether the LAO analysis states outright that a recalled officer can run in the special election, and I'm also noting the Governor succession clause in Article V, Section 10(b), which carves out an exception to Section 15(c).

I'm reading the Governor succession clause in Article V, Section 10(b), which opens with "notwithstanding" Section 15(c). If the Governor is recalled before the nomination period for the next statewide election in the first two years of the term, a special election is consolidated with the primary, and a majority winner takes over, or the top two go to a consolidated general runoff.

I'm checking how the early-term Governor clause sits with the general rule: the Lieutenant Governor takes over on recall, but the next sentences carve out the case where a special election is called instead. In that early-term case, a majority winner in the consolidated primary serves the rest of the term, and if no one gets a majority, the top two face off in a runoff with the November general.

I'm checking whether the Lieutenant Governor serves in the gap between a recall and the special election, and the text doesn't settle that directly. The LAO and Yes campaign materials both seem to say the LG holds the office until a successor is elected, which is what I need to confirm against the LAO summary.

The Yes side's summary says the governor's succession works differently early in the term: if a recall happens before nominations close for the next statewide election, a special election is consolidated with the primary, and the lieutenant governor serves until voters pick a successor. I want to check how that matches the LAO's wording that the lieutenant governor serves "until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election."

I'm thinking through the Governor succession rule, which is one place where the LG's separate election matters. A late-term recall would hand the office to a lieutenant governor who may come from a different party and was never voted in as the top of the ticket. I want to weigh that against the usual logic of having the next official in line take over.

Next I'm checking how the statewide vacancy rule for offices other than Governor works, since the Governor's succession is already clear to me.

I'm turning to the statewide offices other than Governor, where the appointment route matters more than the recall itself. Under the existing rules, a vacancy in those offices gets filled by a Governor's appointee who serves until the next general election. So a recalled Attorney General or Secretary of State would be replaced by someone the Governor picks, not by voters, which is the substitution the opponents are pointing to.

I'm weighing the statewide offices other than Governor, where a recalled official would be replaced by a Governor's appointee serving until the next general election rather than by voters. That would mean a recalled insurance commissioner could be swapped for someone the Governor picks, possibly for a long stretch if the recall happens early, and I still need to see how the Yes side's answer finishes describing the replacement process.

Claude's point is that Prop 5 is less likely to produce a Republican replacement in statewide races, since a Democratic governor would make the appointment, while a Democratic lieutenant governor would take over if the governor were recalled. That gives the measure a partisan lean, though the critics' concern is worth weighing against the measure's neutral text.

I'm checking how the Mercury News frames its objection, since its "No" editorial argues Prop 5 would make it harder for independent-minded challengers to win and would protect the status quo. I still need to pull the actual endorsement text to confirm that wording.

Now I'm weighing the editorial endorsements, starting with the Mercury News, which opposes Prop 5 on the grounds that it protects the status quo, and checking how the LA Times board compares.

I'm going to look for a more recent poll, since the PPIC numbers are from September, and I also want the California Republican Party's position on Prop 5. Next I'll check campaign finance for the Yes committee to see how strong the campaign is.

I'm weighing the replacement rule itself: a recalled official is currently replaced by whoever wins a plurality in a crowded field, as Schwarzenegger did in 2003, while Prop 5 would require a majority. That makes the replacement more democratically legitimate, and it also removes the incentive for partisan recalls to install a candidate who couldn't win a normal election.

I'm checking Ling Ling Chang's replacement win in the 2018 Newman recall, where I think she took the seat with a plurality in the replacement vote rather than a majority, which would fit the point that plurality replacement is the loophole Prop 5 would close.

I'm weighing the case for Prop 5 as well: it would drop the plurality replacement route, so a recalled official would need a majority to be replaced, and the Yes side and several endorsers, including the Secretary of State and the LA Times, point to that as the main benefit. The opposing argument, that voters lose direct say over who replaces a statewide official, still needs weighing against it.

Now I'm weighing the downsides of Prop 5 on the other side: the Governor would gain appointment power over other statewide offices until the next election, and a recalled legislator's special election would cost money, run for months, and let the recalled official run again. The late-term Lieutenant Governor succession also swaps voter choice for a successor from a different party, which critics call tainted.

I'm weighing the measure's "majority rule" pitch, which only partly holds up: statewide appointments by the Governor sidestep it, though legislative special-election runoffs do deliver majority winners. I also notice the signature threshold stays low and Prop 5 doesn't touch it, which is the reform the SF Chronicle thinks lawmakers should have pursued instead.

I'm weighing the measure's downsides, and noting that the Mercury News argues it protects incumbents and shuts out independent challengers, which is the main critique I still have to set against the majority-rule argument.

Now I'm weighing the decision itself: the Chronicle and Mercury News lean No, the LA Times and the good-government groups lean Yes, and the polling currently favors No, so it's a close call.

I'm checking Elder's share of the 2021 replacement vote against the Yes side's "28% of recall voters" claim, since the two numbers may measure different things.

I'm trying to pin down Elder's share of the 2021 replacement vote, since I'm not sure whether the 48% figure I half-remember is right. The Yes side's "28% of recall voters" figure may be measuring something different, so I'll check the Secretary of State's results to compare the two numbers.

I'm weighing the case for Prop 5's benefits against its costs, starting with the claim that it would end plurality replacement in state-level recalls. Under the measure, legislative and early-term gubernatorial vacancies would be filled by majority in a special election, but a late-term gubernatorial succession would still go to the Lieutenant Governor.

I'm weighing the remaining benefits of Prop 5: it would make replacement by majority rather than plurality, which lowers the payoff for targeted recalls and could reduce how often they happen. I'm also noting that it would drop the confusing two-question ballot and might save money in some cases, though the net cost is unclear.

I'm weighing the costs of Prop 5 next: replacing a statewide official by appointment would take away direct voter say, though an appointee would only serve until the next scheduled election, so the effect might be modest. For legislative recalls, the special election would bring added cost and a gap in representation of several months, which the LAO puts at millions of dollars, and I'm checking CalMatters' note on how quickly the governor would have to call it.

I'm weighing the cost of a legislative recall under Prop 5: the seat would sit empty for several months until a special election, where today the replacement is named right away. I'm also noting the design flaw the SF Chronicle flagged, that the recalled official could run again in that special election and possibly win back the seat, which would cut against the point of the recall.

I'm weighing whether the special election's cost to the recalled official's ability to run again and retake the seat, with the leftover recall-related donations, is a fair democratic outcome or a design flaw. Next I'm considering the late-term governor succession, where the Lieutenant Governor would take over for the rest of the term instead of a voter-chosen replacement.

I'm now weighing the partisan side of Prop 5: it would make it harder for a recall to swap a Democratic statewide official for a Republican, which is why Republicans oppose it and Democrats, who sponsored it, support it. We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system.
Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official.

I'm pulling up the actual wording of Prop 5 from the Secretary of State, starting with the amendment to Section 15 of Article II. The recall clause says that if a majority votes to recall, the officer is removed, and the candidate with a plurality takes over, but the officer can't run and the office stays vacant.

I'm checking the rest of the Section 15(c) wording: the vacancy gets filled under the Constitution and statute, but the officer who was recalled can't be appointed to fill it.

I'm working through the text of the amendment and trying to separate the struck language from the new insertions, since the extraction doesn't mark which is which. The open question is whether the ban on the officer running for the office is being kept or removed.

The sources I'm citing all describe the current ban as one the constitution imposes on the recalled officer running in the replacement election, so the struck language is probably the "may not be a candidate" sentence. That would fit the new insertion barring only appointment, not candidacy.

I'm checking how the Section 16(d) reference fits in: the text seems to be striking the ban on a candidacy for a legislative vacancy filled by special election, and I'm not sure yet whether that clause is being kept or removed.

I'm weighing whether the recall text bars candidacy for a special election under Article VI, Section 16(d), and what that clause would mean for the replacement candidate. It reads oddly, so I'm checking whether the prohibition covers running in the legislative special election for the same seat.

I'm going to check whether the LAO analysis states outright that a recalled officer can run in the special election, and I'm also noting the Governor succession clause in Article V, Section 10(b), which carves out an exception to Section 15(c).

I'm reading the Governor succession clause in Article V, Section 10(b), which opens with "notwithstanding" Section 15(c). If the Governor is recalled before the nomination period for the next statewide election in the first two years of the term, a special election is consolidated with the primary, and a majority winner takes over, or the top two go to a consolidated general runoff.

I'm checking how the early-term Governor clause sits with the general rule: the Lieutenant Governor takes over on recall, but the next sentences carve out the case where a special election is called instead. In that early-term case, a majority winner in the consolidated primary serves the rest of the term, and if no one gets a majority, the top two face off in a runoff with the November general.

I'm checking whether the Lieutenant Governor serves in the gap between a recall and the special election, and the text doesn't settle that directly. The LAO and Yes campaign materials both seem to say the LG holds the office until a successor is elected, which is what I need to confirm against the LAO summary.

The Yes side's summary says the governor's succession works differently early in the term: if a recall happens before nominations close for the next statewide election, a special election is consolidated with the primary, and the lieutenant governor serves until voters pick a successor. I want to check how that matches the LAO's wording that the lieutenant governor serves "until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election."

I'm thinking through the Governor succession rule, which is one place where the LG's separate election matters. A late-term recall would hand the office to a lieutenant governor who may come from a different party and was never voted in as the top of the ticket. I want to weigh that against the usual logic of having the next official in line take over.

Next I'm checking how the statewide vacancy rule for offices other than Governor works, since the Governor's succession is already clear to me.

I'm turning to the statewide offices other than Governor, where the appointment route matters more than the recall itself. Under the existing rules, a vacancy in those offices gets filled by a Governor's appointee who serves until the next general election. So a recalled Attorney General or Secretary of State would be replaced by someone the Governor picks, not by voters, which is the substitution the opponents are pointing to.

I'm weighing the statewide offices other than Governor, where a recalled official would be replaced by a Governor's appointee serving until the next general election rather than by voters. That would mean a recalled insurance commissioner could be swapped for someone the Governor picks, possibly for a long stretch if the recall happens early, and I still need to see how the Yes side's answer finishes describing the replacement process.

Claude's point is that Prop 5 is less likely to produce a Republican replacement in statewide races, since a Democratic governor would make the appointment, while a Democratic lieutenant governor would take over if the governor were recalled. That gives the measure a partisan lean, though the critics' concern is worth weighing against the measure's neutral text.

I'm checking how the Mercury News frames its objection, since its "No" editorial argues Prop 5 would make it harder for independent-minded challengers to win and would protect the status quo. I still need to pull the actual endorsement text to confirm that wording.

Now I'm weighing the editorial endorsements, starting with the Mercury News, which opposes Prop 5 on the grounds that it protects the status quo, and checking how the LA Times board compares.

I'm going to look for a more recent poll, since the PPIC numbers are from September, and I also want the California Republican Party's position on Prop 5. Next I'll check campaign finance for the Yes committee to see how strong the campaign is.

I'm weighing the replacement rule itself: a recalled official is currently replaced by whoever wins a plurality in a crowded field, as Schwarzenegger did in 2003, while Prop 5 would require a majority. That makes the replacement more democratically legitimate, and it also removes the incentive for partisan recalls to install a candidate who couldn't win a normal election.

I'm checking Ling Ling Chang's replacement win in the 2018 Newman recall, where I think she took the seat with a plurality in the replacement vote rather than a majority, which would fit the point that plurality replacement is the loophole Prop 5 would close.

I'm weighing the case for Prop 5 as well: it would drop the plurality replacement route, so a recalled official would need a majority to be replaced, and the Yes side and several endorsers, including the Secretary of State and the LA Times, point to that as the main benefit. The opposing argument, that voters lose direct say over who replaces a statewide official, still needs weighing against it.

Now I'm weighing the downsides of Prop 5 on the other side: the Governor would gain appointment power over other statewide offices until the next election, and a recalled legislator's special election would cost money, run for months, and let the recalled official run again. The late-term Lieutenant Governor succession also swaps voter choice for a successor from a different party, which critics call tainted.

I'm weighing the measure's "majority rule" pitch, which only partly holds up: statewide appointments by the Governor sidestep it, though legislative special-election runoffs do deliver majority winners. I also notice the signature threshold stays low and Prop 5 doesn't touch it, which is the reform the SF Chronicle thinks lawmakers should have pursued instead.

I'm weighing the measure's downsides, and noting that the Mercury News argues it protects incumbents and shuts out independent challengers, which is the main critique I still have to set against the majority-rule argument.

Now I'm weighing the decision itself: the Chronicle and Mercury News lean No, the LA Times and the good-government groups lean Yes, and the polling currently favors No, so it's a close call.

I'm checking Elder's share of the 2021 replacement vote against the Yes side's "28% of recall voters" claim, since the two numbers may measure different things.

I'm trying to pin down Elder's share of the 2021 replacement vote, since I'm not sure whether the 48% figure I half-remember is right. The Yes side's "28% of recall voters" figure may be measuring something different, so I'll check the Secretary of State's results to compare the two numbers.

I'm weighing the case for Prop 5's benefits against its costs, starting with the claim that it would end plurality replacement in state-level recalls. Under the measure, legislative and early-term gubernatorial vacancies would be filled by majority in a special election, but a late-term gubernatorial succession would still go to the Lieutenant Governor.

I'm weighing the remaining benefits of Prop 5: it would make replacement by majority rather than plurality, which lowers the payoff for targeted recalls and could reduce how often they happen. I'm also noting that it would drop the confusing two-question ballot and might save money in some cases, though the net cost is unclear.

I'm weighing the costs of Prop 5 next: replacing a statewide official by appointment would take away direct voter say, though an appointee would only serve until the next scheduled election, so the effect might be modest. For legislative recalls, the special election would bring added cost and a gap in representation of several months, which the LAO puts at millions of dollars, and I'm checking CalMatters' note on how quickly the governor would have to call it.

I'm weighing the cost of a legislative recall under Prop 5: the seat would sit empty for several months until a special election, where today the replacement is named right away. I'm also noting the design flaw the SF Chronicle flagged, that the recalled official could run again in that special election and possibly win back the seat, which would cut against the point of the recall.

I'm weighing whether the special election's cost to the recalled official's ability to run again and retake the seat, with the leftover recall-related donations, is a fair democratic outcome or a design flaw. Next I'm considering the late-term governor succession, where the Lieutenant Governor would take over for the rest of the term instead of a voter-chosen replacement.

I'm now weighing the partisan side of Prop 5: it would make it harder for a recall to swap a Democratic statewide official for a Republican, which is why Republicans oppose it and Democrats, who sponsored it, support it. Whether that partisan effect counts as a benefit or a cost depends on which side of the recall you're on.

I'm weighing the measure's merits separately from the partisan motives behind it. I also note that the ballot title is misleading since it covers legislative seats too, and that the constitutional change would be hard to undo if its design turns out flawed. The low signature threshold goes untouched, which means the measure is at best a partial fix.

I'm now weighing the editorial positions: the SF Chronicle and Mercury News recommend No, pointing to the recalled official's ability to run again and the loss of voter choice in replacement, while the LWV, Common Cause, and other advocates back Yes. I still need to confirm where the LA Times editorial board actually stands.

I'm weighing the pro case for Prop 5: the plurality replacement rule is the main loophole, and majority rule plus less incentive for partisan recalls, backed by good-government groups and the Secretary of State, carry real weight. I also want to check the 2021 numbers, since the Yes side's claim that the leading replacement had only about 28% of recall voters may be measuring something different from the replacement vote share.

I'm checking Schwarzenegger's 2003 result, where he won about 48.6% of the replacement vote among 135 candidates, which is a large plurality rather than a thin one. That makes me wonder whether plurality winners still tend to have broad support, even though the Yes side frames the replacement share as small.

I'm checking the 2021 replacement numbers against the Yes side's claim that Elder would have won with only about 28% of recall voters, since the share of the replacement vote I half-remember may be a different measure altogether.

Next I'm checking Elder's 2021 replacement share, since the Yes side's 28%-of-recall-voters figure may not match the replacement vote numbers I half-remember. I'll search for the official results to settle it.

I'm planning the next checks: the LAO analysis on the recalled official's candidacy and the special election timeline, the Mercury News and LA Times editorial positions, the other papers' endorsements, the latest PPIC and Berkeley IGS polls, party stances, and the 2021 and 2018 replacement vote shares, starting with Elder's figure.

I'm planning the next searches: fetching the official 2021 and 2003 replacement results to settle Elder's share, plus the Prop 5 fundraising totals and the Mercury News and LA Times editorial positions.

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)

This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.
Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time.
Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021.
The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.
Where Prop. 5 came from
In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office.
Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win.
They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections.
Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker.
Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003.

California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.
Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time.

Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021.
The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.
Where Prop. 5 came from
In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office.
Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win.
They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections.
Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker.
Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003.

# Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide.
Such elections have been rare in California.
...
If Prop.
5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled.
If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held.
If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor.
Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until a special election was held.
If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop.
5.

## What a ‘yes’ vote means
If enacted by voters, the ballot measure bars voters from naming a successor to a position if the current officeholder is recalled in the same election.
Instead, the office would be filled at a later date either via a special election or appointment.
Prop.
5 would also remove a ban on recalled leaders running for the same office they had been recalled from, but they would not be able to be appointed to that position.
For example, if the ballot measure were in effect and the governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take their place until a successor was picked in a special election.

California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.
Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time.
Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021.
The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.
Where Prop. 5 came from
In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office.
Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win.
They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections.
Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker.
Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003.

Proposition 5 seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide.
Such elections have been rare in California.

If Prop.

In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled.
If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held.
If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor.
Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until a special election was held.
If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.

California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms. Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes. Where Prop. 5 came from In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker. Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003. READ NEXT Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections. To help you make decisions about the 14 statewide propositions on California's ballot, our opinion team made recommendations like it does for every election. The process is completely separate from newsroom reporting and journalists.
But the team considers arguments from across the political spectrum while developing its editorial stance. We understand that not everyone will agree with these endorsements – that's the nature of politics.
If you’d rather read impartial articles from our reporters, they covered all 14 propositions in this guide: All 14 propositions before California voters this year, explained (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/07/02/election-2026-all-14-propositions-before-california-voters-this-year-explained/)
We hope it helps you clarify your own reason for choosing how to vote.
Tax-related💲
❌ No on Prop 2, California's rainy day fund: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-no-on-prop-2-california-needs-fiscal-discipline-not-accounting-tricks/)Prop. 2 would double the state budget reserve cap from 10% of General Fund revenues to 20% of General Fund revenues. The General Fund is the state's main spending account.
❌ No on Prop 3, Income tax rates: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/02/endorsement-no-on-proposition-3-temporary-taxes-should-be-temporary/)Prop 3 would extend the state’s highest income tax rates, which are now up to 12% for single filers who earn more than $360,000 per year and other high income groups, past 2031.
❌ No on Prop 40, One-time tax on billionaires: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/)This measure, known as the "Billionaire Tax Act," would enact a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires to raise temporary revenue to address the loss of federal funding to health, nutrition, and education services, largely a result of the 2025 budget reconciliation law known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill."
✅ Yes on Prop 41, Audits and limitations on special taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/21/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-41-and-42-to-limit-taxation-in-california/)Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. It would also require new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit - the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year, therefore blocking Prop 40, the "Billionaire Tax."
✅ Yes on Prop 42, Ban on new personal property taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/21/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-41-and-42-to-limit-taxation-in-california/)Prop 42 is another attempt to block Prop 40, this time by prohibiting new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property. California doesn't currently tax financial assets, and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees).
Government & Election Reform 🏛️
❌ No on Prop 4, Expansion of public campaign financing programs: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)Prop 4 would lift a ban that keeps counties, districts, most cities and the state from giving candidates public funds to run for election if they agree to certain terms. Cities won't automatically offer the program, but they would have that option.
❌ No on Prop 5, Changes to recall elections of state officials: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)This measure would make state recall elections just a yes or no question and remove the "Who should replace them?" query. If the governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would fill the role, and for other state offices, vacancies would be filled according to state law.
✅ Yes on Prop 39, Voter ID for future elections: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/15/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-39/)Prop 39 would change the current protocol by requiring all voters to show ID when voting in person or provide the last four digits of their ID number when voting by mail. Election officials would also be required to report the percentage of county voters whose citizenship has been verified.
✅ Yes on Prop 43, New threshold for passing local taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)Right now, it takes 50% of voters to approve a local tax that appears on a ballot through the signature-gathering process. If Prop. 43 passed, it would raise that threshold to 75% for a new tax, a tax increase or an extension to be implemented.
Housing & Social Infrastructure 🏡
❌ No on Prop 1, Veterans and affordable housing bonds: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/23/endorsement-no-on-prop-1-more-debt-wont-fix-californias-housing-shortage/)This measure would allow the state to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to fund affordable housing efforts.
❌ No on Prop 37, Home loans to middle-income earners: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/)Prop 37 would let the state issue $25 billion in bonds to help middle-income homebuyers afford homes.
❌ No on Prop 38, Immunology and immunotherapy research: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/23/endorsement-no-on-proposition-38-an-8-4-billion-money-grab/)Prop 38 would approve $8.4 billion in bonds toward California nonprofit universities' medical research into treatments that use the body's own immune system to treat disease.
❌ No on Prop 44, Community clinic spending: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/08/endorsement-no-on-proposition-44-a-cynical-attack-on-community-health-clinics/)Prop 44 would make it so safety-net health clinics must spend 90% of their revenue on providing services to underserved people, rather than on management.
✅ Yes on Prop 45, Changes to CEQA (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/09/endorsement-yes-on-prop-45-to-reform-ceqa/) (California Environmental Quality Act): Prop 45 would speed up California's environmental impact review process for certain projects like housing, transportation and infrastructure by limiting its scope and setting review deadlines for public agencies.

California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms. Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes. Where Prop. 5 came from In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker. Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?

By Kate Wolffe, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.

Proposition 5 would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. 

Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. 

The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it, while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.

Where Prop. 5 came from

In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. 

Weber and good governance groups argued the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. 

They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms. Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes. Where Prop. 5 came from In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker. Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. By Kate Wolffe, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.

If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. 

Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021.

2026 Election: California Ballot proposition endorsements from our opinion team could help make tough choices
By Teagan Davidge, The Orange County Register
The Tribune Content Agency
October 20, 2026 5:41 PM
Voters have through Nov. 3 to cast their ballots, but election officials are especially encouraging those who vote by mail to do so early. (Photo by Mark Rightmire, Orange County Register/SCNG)
Mark Rightmire
TNS
To help you make decisions about the 14 statewide propositions on California's ballot, our opinion team made recommendations like it does for every election. The process is completely separate from newsroom reporting and journalists.
But the team considers arguments from across the political spectrum while developing its editorial stance. We understand that not everyone will agree with these endorsements – that's the nature of politics.
If you’d rather read impartial articles from our reporters, they covered all 14 propositions in this guide: All 14 propositions before California voters this year, explained (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/07/02/election-2026-all-14-propositions-before-california-voters-this-year-explained/)
We hope it helps you clarify your own reason for choosing how to vote.
Tax-related💲
❌ No on Prop 2, California's rainy day fund: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-no-on-prop-2-california-needs-fiscal-discipline-not-accounting-tricks/)Prop. 2 would double the state budget reserve cap from 10% of General Fund revenues to 20% of General Fund revenues. The General Fund is the state's main spending account.
❌ No on Prop 3, Income tax rates: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/02/endorsement-no-on-proposition-3-temporary-taxes-should-be-temporary/)Prop 3 would extend the state’s highest income tax rates, which are now up to 12% for single filers who earn more than $360,000 per year and other high income groups, past 2031.
❌ No on Prop 40, One-time tax on billionaires: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/)This measure, known as the "Billionaire Tax Act," would enact a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires to raise temporary revenue to address the loss of federal funding to health, nutrition, and education services, largely a result of the 2025 budget reconciliation law known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill."
✅ Yes on Prop 41, Audits and limitations on special taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/21/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-41-and-42-to-limit-taxation-in-california/)Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. It would also require new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit - the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year, therefore blocking Prop 40, the "Billionaire Tax."
✅ Yes on Prop 42, Ban on new personal property taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/21/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-41-and-42-to-limit-taxation-in-california/)Prop 42 is another attempt to block Prop 40, this time by prohibiting new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property. California doesn't currently tax financial assets, and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees).
Government & Election Reform 🏛️
❌ No on Prop 4, Expansion of public campaign financing programs: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)Prop 4 would lift a ban that keeps counties, districts, most cities and the state from giving candidates public funds to run for election if they agree to certain terms. Cities won't automatically offer the program, but they would have that option.
❌ No on Prop 5, Changes to recall elections of state officials: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)This measure would make state recall elections just a yes or no question and remove the "Who should replace them?" query. If the governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would fill the role, and for other state offices, vacancies would be filled according to state law.
✅ Yes on Prop 39, Voter ID for future elections: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/15/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-39/)Prop 39 would change the current protocol by requiring all voters to show ID when voting in person or provide the last four digits of their ID number when voting by mail. Election officials would also be required to report the percentage of county voters whose citizenship has been verified.
✅ Yes on Prop 43, New threshold for passing local taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)Right now, it takes 50% of voters to approve a local tax that appears on a ballot through the signature-gathering process. If Prop. 43 passed, it would raise that threshold to 75% for a new tax, a tax increase or an extension to be implemented.
Housing & Social Infrastructure 🏡
❌ No on Prop 1, Veterans and affordable housing bonds: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/23/endorsement-no-on-prop-1-more-debt-wont-fix-californias-housing-shortage/)This measure would allow the state to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to fund affordable housing efforts.
