2026 Election: California Ballot proposition endorsements from our opinion team could help make tough choices
By Teagan Davidge, The Orange County Register
The Tribune Content Agency
October 20, 2026 5:41 PM
Voters have through Nov. 3 to cast their ballots, but election officials are especially encouraging those who vote by mail to do so early. (Photo by Mark Rightmire, Orange County Register/SCNG)
Mark Rightmire
TNS
To help you make decisions about the 14 statewide propositions on California's ballot, our opinion team made recommendations like it does for every election. The process is completely separate from newsroom reporting and journalists.
But the team considers arguments from across the political spectrum while developing its editorial stance. We understand that not everyone will agree with these endorsements – that's the nature of politics.
If you’d rather read impartial articles from our reporters, they covered all 14 propositions in this guide: All 14 propositions before California voters this year, explained (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/07/02/election-2026-all-14-propositions-before-california-voters-this-year-explained/)
We hope it helps you clarify your own reason for choosing how to vote.
Tax-related💲
❌ No on Prop 2, California's rainy day fund: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-no-on-prop-2-california-needs-fiscal-discipline-not-accounting-tricks/)Prop. 2 would double the state budget reserve cap from 10% of General Fund revenues to 20% of General Fund revenues. The General Fund is the state's main spending account.
❌ No on Prop 3, Income tax rates: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/02/endorsement-no-on-proposition-3-temporary-taxes-should-be-temporary/)Prop 3 would extend the state’s highest income tax rates, which are now up to 12% for single filers who earn more than $360,000 per year and other high income groups, past 2031.
❌ No on Prop 40, One-time tax on billionaires: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/)This measure, known as the "Billionaire Tax Act," would enact a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires to raise temporary revenue to address the loss of federal funding to health, nutrition, and education services, largely a result of the 2025 budget reconciliation law known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill."
✅ Yes on Prop 41, Audits and limitations on special taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/21/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-41-and-42-to-limit-taxation-in-california/)Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. It would also require new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit - the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year, therefore blocking Prop 40, the "Billionaire Tax."
✅ Yes on Prop 42, Ban on new personal property taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/21/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-41-and-42-to-limit-taxation-in-california/)Prop 42 is another attempt to block Prop 40, this time by prohibiting new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property. California doesn't currently tax financial assets, and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees).
Government & Election Reform 🏛️
❌ No on Prop 4, Expansion of public campaign financing programs: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)Prop 4 would lift a ban that keeps counties, districts, most cities and the state from giving candidates public funds to run for election if they agree to certain terms. Cities won't automatically offer the program, but they would have that option.
❌ No on Prop 5, Changes to recall elections of state officials: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)This measure would make state recall elections just a yes or no question and remove the "Who should replace them?" query. If the governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would fill the role, and for other state offices, vacancies would be filled according to state law.
✅ Yes on Prop 39, Voter ID for future elections: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/15/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-39/)Prop 39 would change the current protocol by requiring all voters to show ID when voting in person or provide the last four digits of their ID number when voting by mail. Election officials would also be required to report the percentage of county voters whose citizenship has been verified.
✅ Yes on Prop 43, New threshold for passing local taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)Right now, it takes 50% of voters to approve a local tax that appears on a ballot through the signature-gathering process. If Prop. 43 passed, it would raise that threshold to 75% for a new tax, a tax increase or an extension to be implemented.
Housing & Social Infrastructure 🏡
❌ No on Prop 1, Veterans and affordable housing bonds: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/23/endorsement-no-on-prop-1-more-debt-wont-fix-californias-housing-shortage/)This measure would allow the state to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to fund affordable housing efforts.
❌ No on Prop 37, Home loans to middle-income earners: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/)Prop 37 would let the state issue $25 billion in bonds to help middle-income homebuyers afford homes.
❌ No on Prop 38, Immunology and immunotherapy research: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/23/endorsement-no-on-proposition-38-an-8-4-billion-money-grab/)Prop 38 would approve $8.4 billion in bonds toward California nonprofit universities' medical research into treatments that use the body's own immune system to treat disease.
❌ No on Prop 44, Community clinic spending: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/08/endorsement-no-on-proposition-44-a-cynical-attack-on-community-health-clinics/)Prop 44 would make it so safety-net health clinics must spend 90% of their revenue on providing services to underserved people, rather than on management.
✅ Yes on Prop 45, Changes to CEQA (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/09/endorsement-yes-on-prop-45-to-reform-ceqa/) (California Environmental Quality Act): Prop 45 would speed up California's environmental impact review process for certain projects like housing, transportation and infrastructure by limiting its scope and setting review deadlines for public agencies.

California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms. Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes. Where Prop. 5 came from In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker. Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003. READ NEXT Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections. By Teagan Davidge, The Orange County Register
The Tribune Content Agency
October 20, 2026 5:41 PM
Voters have through Nov. 3 to cast their ballots, but election officials are especially encouraging those who vote by mail to do so early. (Photo by Mark Rightmire, Orange County Register/SCNG)
Mark Rightmire
TNS
To help you make decisions about the 14 statewide propositions on California's ballot, our opinion team made recommendations like it does for every election. The process is completely separate from newsroom reporting and journalists.
But the team considers arguments from across the political spectrum while developing its editorial stance. We understand that not everyone will agree with these endorsements – that's the nature of politics.
If you’d rather read impartial articles from our reporters, they covered all 14 propositions in this guide: All 14 propositions before California voters this year, explained (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/07/02/election-2026-all-14-propositions-before-california-voters-this-year-explained/)
We hope it helps you clarify your own reason for choosing how to vote.
Tax-related💲
❌ No on Prop 2, California's rainy day fund: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-no-on-prop-2-california-needs-fiscal-discipline-not-accounting-tricks/)Prop. 2 would double the state budget reserve cap from 10% of General Fund revenues to 20% of General Fund revenues. The General Fund is the state's main spending account.
❌ No on Prop 3, Income tax rates: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/02/endorsement-no-on-proposition-3-temporary-taxes-should-be-temporary/)Prop 3 would extend the state’s highest income tax rates, which are now up to 12% for single filers who earn more than $360,000 per year and other high income groups, past 2031.
❌ No on Prop 40, One-time tax on billionaires: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/)This measure, known as the "Billionaire Tax Act," would enact a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires to raise temporary revenue to address the loss of federal funding to health, nutrition, and education services, largely a result of the 2025 budget reconciliation law known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill."
✅ Yes on Prop 41, Audits and limitations on special taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/21/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-41-and-42-to-limit-taxation-in-california/)Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. It would also require new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit - the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year, therefore blocking Prop 40, the "Billionaire Tax."
✅ Yes on Prop 42, Ban on new personal property taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/21/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-41-and-42-to-limit-taxation-in-california/)Prop 42 is another attempt to block Prop 40, this time by prohibiting new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property. California doesn't currently tax financial assets, and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees).
Government & Election Reform 🏛️
❌ No on Prop 4, Expansion of public campaign financing programs: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)Prop 4 would lift a ban that keeps counties, districts, most cities and the state from giving candidates public funds to run for election if they agree to certain terms. Cities won't automatically offer the program, but they would have that option.
❌ No on Prop 5, Changes to recall elections of state officials: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)This measure would make state recall elections just a yes or no question and remove the "Who should replace them?" query. If the governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would fill the role, and for other state offices, vacancies would be filled according to state law.
✅ Yes on Prop 39, Voter ID for future elections: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/15/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-39/)Prop 39 would change the current protocol by requiring all voters to show ID when voting in person or provide the last four digits of their ID number when voting by mail. Election officials would also be required to report the percentage of county voters whose citizenship has been verified.
✅ Yes on Prop 43, New threshold for passing local taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)Right now, it takes 50% of voters to approve a local tax that appears on a ballot through the signature-gathering process. If Prop. 43 passed, it would raise that threshold to 75% for a new tax, a tax increase or an extension to be implemented.
Housing & Social Infrastructure 🏡
❌ No on Prop 1, Veterans and affordable housing bonds: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/23/endorsement-no-on-prop-1-more-debt-wont-fix-californias-housing-shortage/)This measure would allow the state to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to fund affordable housing efforts.
❌ No on Prop 37, Home loans to middle-income earners: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/)Prop 37 would let the state issue $25 billion in bonds to help middle-income homebuyers afford homes.
❌ No on Prop 38, Immunology and immunotherapy research: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/23/endorsement-no-on-proposition-38-an-8-4-billion-money-grab/)Prop 38 would approve $8.4 billion in bonds toward California nonprofit universities' medical research into treatments that use the body's own immune system to treat disease.
❌ No on Prop 44, Community clinic spending: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/08/endorsement-no-on-proposition-44-a-cynical-attack-on-community-health-clinics/)Prop 44 would make it so safety-net health clinics must spend 90% of their revenue on providing services to underserved people, rather than on management.
✅ Yes on Prop 45, Changes to CEQA (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/09/endorsement-yes-on-prop-45-to-reform-ceqa/) (California Environmental Quality Act): Prop 45 would speed up California's environmental impact review process for certain projects like housing, transportation and infrastructure by limiting its scope and setting review deadlines for public agencies.

California voters will decide on whether the state's recall election process will change.
Proposition 5 could make removing an elected official from office as simple as answering one ballot question. Currently, a recall requires voters to decide whether or not a politician should be removed, then answer who should replace them. 2026 elections: Track results for California Proposition 5
Nijzel Dotson
Digital Producer
California voters will decide on whether the state's recall election process will change.
Proposition 5 could make removing an elected official from office as simple as answering one ballot question. Currently, a recall requires voters to decide whether or not a politician should be removed, then answer who should replace them. If passed, Prop 5 would remove the current second section, which would mean voters would be asked to elect a sucessor in a separate process.

Now I'm weighing the 2018 Newman recall, where Chang came out ahead with about 33.8% of the replacement votes in a six-way race, and I'm double-checking that figure against the Secretary of State's table.

I'm now comparing Chang's 33.8% plurality in the 2018 recall replacement against Newman's 58.1% recall vote, and working out how her share of total district voters comes out, which lands around 32%. The field was crowded, with three Democrats splitting the vote, so the winner's share was low and the head-to-head outcome in a general election would look different.

The plurality logic is the key point here: Chang won with about 34% because the Democratic vote was split three ways. Looking at the parties, Republicans combined for roughly 58% of the replacement votes and Democrats for about 42%, so the winner's plurality didn't go against the party majority in this field, even though a head-to-head result could have looked different.

I'm looking at how Chang's 33.8% plurality would have fared in a top-two runoff against Cho, and whether it would have changed the result. Republicans together held a majority of the replacement votes, so a runoff might well have kept Chang in office, though that is not certain.

Now I'm noting the San Diego Union-Tribune's No position from September 25, which argues the measure is a power play by the Democratic establishment to keep Republicans and independents from winning governor through recall. Press-Enterprise, OC Register, and LA Daily News have all come out against it too.

I'm checking whether the Southern California News Group papers all took the same No position, since the OC Register and Press-Enterprise ran identical editorial text on August 12. The LA Daily News is also part of that group, so its No recommendation fits the pattern, though I haven't confirmed it directly.

I'm checking the editorial positions across the major papers now. The NO side includes the SF Chronicle, the Mercury News, the San Diego Union-Tribune, and the Southern California News Group papers, while the YES side has the McClatchy papers and a couple of LA Times columnists, with the LA Times board taking no position.

I'm noting the Republican leaders in the Senate and Assembly, plus the Sacramento Bee's reference to top California Republicans, all opposing the measure, while the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Secretary of State, the state Democratic Party, and good-government groups back it. The newspaper tally leans No, but the polling is close, with October PPIC showing 45% yes and 52% no among likely voters.

I'm weighing the 2018 Newman case, where a 34% plurality winner shows the flaw in the current system, against the arguments for No: the drafting problems, the appointment power, and the succession issues.

I'm now weighing whether the plurality flaw is really a flaw in the democratic sense, since a winner with 33.8% in a six-way field means most voters preferred someone else, though vote-splitting among opponents is part of the picture too. California's regular system avoids this through top-two primaries and head-to-head general elections, while special elections use a special primary and special general that aim for majority winners, so that's the comparison I need to keep in view.

I'm weighing the Yes argument that Prop 5 would bring recall replacements in line with the rest of California's elections, where top-two general contests already require a majority winner. The No side's case that voters should choose replacements directly still holds, though under Prop 5 they would still do that in special elections.

I'm weighing whether the candidacy drafting problem matters much in practice, since it only affects special elections. For a late-term governor recall, the lieutenant governor, who is elected statewide, takes over the remaining term, so the replacement still comes from a direct vote, though some good-government advocates would object to that.

I'm now looking at the cost side: special elections for a legislative recall would run into the millions, and the LAO couldn't pin down a net figure, though it's small next to the state budget. Some voters may see that as a fair price for a more legitimate replacement.

I'm now weighing the political-motive charge against the merits: the San Diego Union-Tribune calls the measure a power play, but that's a claim about motive, so the substance has to decide it. On the merits, the Yes case is strong in principle, since it makes recall replacements consistent with California's majority-winner general elections and the 2018 Newman winner took only about 34%. The No case is stronger in its specifics: the candidacy drafting flaw, the appointment and lieutenant governor succession issues, and the costs.

I'm weighing whether a "no" vote, which keeps the plurality loophole open, is worse than a "yes" vote that fixes the core problem but brings some design quirks. The candidacy issue could be corrected later, but amending the constitution would take two-thirds of each house plus a voter majority, so it would likely stay in place for a long time.

I'm now asking whether a flawed but mostly sound measure is better than the status quo. Ballot analysts often default to no when benefits are uncertain and new problems are certain, and the candidacy issue would be hard to fix later since amending the constitution takes two-thirds of each house plus voter approval. I'm leaning toward thinking the core concept is right even though the execution has real problems.

I'm weighing the SF Chronicle's view that a clean reform would be the better route, since a constitutional amendment this flawed would be hard to fix later. The League of Women Voters and Common Cause back the measure too, and as neutral-leaning good-government groups their support carries weight, even though they'd presumably see the candidacy problem and still find it acceptable. Their

Weighing the core benefit against the design problems: majority-based replacements fit California's general-election principle, while the candidacy flaw, appointments, legislative recall costs, and the partisan motive are the main downsides, with only the candidacy issue clearly a bug.

I'm weighing the design bug against the bigger accountability question: under current law a statewide recall installs an immediate plurality winner, while Prop 5 would have the Governor appoint a replacement until the next scheduled election, and I need to check exactly how that appointment works.

I'm checking how an appointed replacement would work for a recalled statewide officer: the Governor would fill the seat until the next scheduled election, which is roughly a year and a half in the example. That's a real but limited loss of direct voter choice. For the lieutenant governor, I still need to pin down whether the appointment requires Senate confirmation.

I'm working through the rest of the succession picture: if the Governor is recalled late in the term, the Lieutenant Governor, who is elected statewide, takes over under the existing constitutional line of succession, so that seems reasonable. For an early-term recall, the Lieutenant Governor only bridges to a special election where voters pick the new Governor by majority, which is a good outcome. The legislative seats get special elections with majority winners too, though the gap and cost remain. On legitimacy, majority special elections look better in the most consequential case, an early-term governor replaced by a plurality winner with only about 25% of the vote.

I'm now seeing that the governor case is where Prop 5 does the most good, since an early-term governor would be chosen by a majority rather than by someone with a quarter or a third of the vote. Legislative seats would get better legitimacy too, but at a real cost in special elections. For statewide offices other than governor, the picture is less clear, since appointments are less direct than a plurality election.

Prop 5 looks like a net improvement for the governor and legislative cases, since majority-based replacements there beat a plurality winner with a quarter of the vote. For statewide offices other than governor, though, appointments give voters less say, so that part cuts the other way. On the merits I lean toward "yes," with the candidacy provision pulling that lean back somewhat.

I'm weighing the governor case more closely now: a recall replacement would hand the job to the lieutenant governor for the months until a special election, which is a real interim cost but an acceptable one. I'm also checking whether a recall could be pushed into a statewide primary, and whether a lieutenant governor from the other party would matter, though that seems rare.

I'm weighing the candidacy provision and the partisan timing against the legitimacy gains, and I'm noticing that a voter who suspects self-serving motives might reasonably vote no as a check on incumbents.

I'm now weighing the partisan asymmetry: the Democratic supermajority placed this amendment, and it removes a plurality route that would mostly help a minority party facing a recall of a Democratic official. Good-government groups back it, but they may not have weighed that angle, so I'm asking whether the asymmetry is a real problem or just how the rules happen to fall.

I'm noting that Republicans can still reach statewide general elections under top-two, as the Hilton example shows, so Prop 5 mainly bites in recall situations. That makes the partisan asymmetry real but narrow. I'm also checking the Legislature's 2024 vote, 32-8 in the Senate and 59-17 in the Assembly, to see how lopsided the placement was.

I'm checking the Legislature's vote counts to see how partisan the placement was. The Senate tally of 32 ayes suggests at least a couple of Republicans joined in, while the Assembly's 59 ayes against 17 noes would mean essentially no Republican support there, with a few Republicans absent.

I'm checking the Senate tally, where 32 ayes could mean two Republicans crossed over, and CalMatters describes the vote as largely Republican opposition. That points to a mostly partisan split, even though good-government groups back the measure. I'm weighing whether that split reflects the technical merits or just how the partisan effect was perceived.

I'm still leaning toward "yes" on the merits, since majority rule and the governor and legislative cases look like real improvements. But the drafting and partisanship concerns keep me from being sure. I want to settle on one answer, so I'm checking whether the recall-candidacy rule is unusual among states.

I'm wondering whether other states let a recalled official run in the replacement election, since if most do, California's candidacy ban looks like the outlier and the SF Chronicle's "unnecessary" claim gets weaker. I'll check how other states handle that and what the LAO says about appointment and recall costs.

I'm going to check how other states handle recalled officials running in the replacement election, since that will show whether California's ban is unusual. I'll also look at the Ballotpedia overview of Proposition 5.

### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

### Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

I've found that California and Colorado are the only two states that bar the officeholder from running on the replacement ballot, according to a 2021 NCSL hearing presentation. I'm now checking how the other states handle the recalled official's name on the replacement ballot.

Many other states let the recalled official run again on the replacement ballot, with Arizona, Nevada, and Wisconsin adding them automatically. That makes California's prohibition look unusual, which weakens the SF Chronicle's claim that the provision is unnecessary.

Prop 5's candidacy change turns out to be the mainstream approach, so California's ban is the outlier rather than the restoration. That undercuts the Chronicle's "bizarre flaw" framing, since only California and Colorado bar the recalled official from the replacement ballot.

The remaining states that hold separate special elections, like Georgia and New Jersey, probably don't bar the recalled official either, so Prop 5's candidacy change looks like the national norm and California's ban is the outlier. The NCSL timeline for legislative vacancy special elections also seems to match Prop 5's roughly four-month window, which would fit the current vacancy process.

Now I'm sorting out how the states that do run separate special elections fit in, along with the two-question versus single-question recall setups.

The NCSL breakdown splits states into groups: seven hold recall and replacement votes simultaneously, including California, while the rest run them as separate steps. That means Prop 5 would shift California toward the separate-election majority, which lines up with the Chronicle's point.

Among the states that hold recall and replacement votes separately, the candidacy ban doesn't appear to be common, so the prohibition looks like California's outlier rather than the norm. Prop 5 would remove it and bring California in line with most other states.

The recalled-official ban looks like California's own quirk rather than a national norm, and that undercuts the Chronicle's point about the replacement ballot. Prop 5's other main choices also track common practice, such as separate replacement votes and succession for vacancies. The 2018 plurality winner at 33.8% is a real flaw, and the measure's majority requirement addresses it, so I'm leaning toward yes.

I'm weighing the "No" side's strongest points: voter choice and direct democracy, partisan optics, the cost of legislative recalls, appointment power, and lieutenant governor succession. The public skepticism and the editorial board majority against it are signals I'll weigh too. Given the national-norm evidence, I'm now leaning toward yes.

I'm going to check the NCSL recall page directly to confirm which states hold recall and replacement votes together and which run them separately, and whether the recalled official can appear on the replacement ballot in the separate-election states. I also want to double-check Colorado's rule and whether California really stands out.

This changes my read on one point. A 2021 California Senate slide, citing NCSL, says only Colorado and California bar the recalled officeholder from the replacement ballot, so Prop 5's candidacy change would bring California in line with most states. I'll verify this against NCSL's own recall page.

Introduction
Overview
History
Process
Key Takeaways
Nineteen states allow recall of state officials, enabling citizens to remove elected officials before their terms end. Virginia has a process that is similar to recall, but involves a recall trial, where a circuit court determines whether to remove an elected official, rather than an election.
Recall processes vary across states, but generally a recall effort involves collecting a certain number of signatures on a petition within a set timeframe. After a petition meeting the requirements is submitted to the appropriate authority and verified, a recall election is held.
NOTE: The following is presented for informational purposes only. NCSL does not provide advice on how to conduct a recall campaign in any state. For the specific procedures to be followed in any state, please contact your state's election official s (https://www.eac.gov/voters/register-and-vote-in-your-state) .
Introduction
In the 19 states that allow state recall elections, citizens can attempt to remove an elected official from office. Typically, the recall process consists of gathering a certain number of signatures on a petition in a certain amount of time. Beyond this, details of the recall process vary by state. This page explains these processes and provides a list of each state's laws governing the recall of state officials.
Overview
Recall is a procedure that allows citizens to remove and replace a public official before the official’s term of office ends. Historically, recall has been used most frequently at the local level. By some estimates, three-fourths of recall elections are at the city council or school board level. This webpage, however, focuses on the recall only as it applies to state officials.
Recall differs from another method for removing officials from office—impeachment (https://www.ncsl.org/about-state-legislatures/separation-of-powers-impeachment)—in that it is a political device while impeachment is a legal process. Impeachment typically requires a state legislature’s lower chamber to bring specific charges, and the upper chamber to act as the jury in an impeachment trial. In contrast, in most of the 19 recall states specific grounds for recall are not required, and the recall of a state official is accomplished through an election.
Nineteen states plus the District of Columbia permit the recall of state officials:
Alaska – Const. Art. 11, §8; Alaska Stat. §15.45.470-15.45.710
Arizona – Const. Art. 8, Pt. 1, §1-6; Ariz. Rev. Stat.
California – Const. Art 2, §13-19; Cal. Elec. Code §11000-11386
Colorado – Const. Art. 21, Colo. Rev. Stat. §1-12-101 – 1-12-123
District of Columbia – D.C. Code §1-1001.17, §1-204.111 et seq.
Georgia – Const. Art. §2, Para. 4; Ga. Code §21-4-1 et seq.
Idaho – Const. Art. 6, §6; Idaho Code §34-1701 – 34-1715
Illinois – Const. Art. 3, §7
Kansas – Const. Art, 4, §3; Kan. Stat. Ann. §25-4301 – 25-4331
Louisiana – Const. Art. 10, §26; La. Stat. Ann. §18:1300.1 - 18:1300.17
Michigan – Const. Art. 2, §8; Mich. Comp. Laws §168.951 - 168.977
Minnesota – Const. Art. 8, §6; Minn. Stat. Ann. §211C.01 et seq.
Montana – Mont. Code Ann. §2-16-601 – 2-16-635
Nevada – Const. Art. 2, §9; Nev. Rev. Stat. §294A.006, §306.005 et seq.
New Jersey – Const. Art. 1, §2(b); N.J. Rev. Stat. Ann. §19:27A-1 – 19:27A-18
North Dakota – Const. Art. 3, §1 and §10; N.D. Cent. Code §16.1-01-09.1
Oregon – Const. Art. 2, §18; Or. Rev. Stat. §249.865 - 249.877
Rhode Island – Const. Art. 4, §1
Washington – Const. Art. 1, Sec. 33-34; Wash Rev. Code §29A.56.110 - 29A.56.270
Wisconsin – Const. Art. 13, §12; Wis. Stat. Ann. §9.10
All these states lay out the right to recall elected officials in their constitutions, with the exception of Montana, where the right to recall is found only in state statutes. Additionally, each recall state except Illinois and Rhode Island further explains its recall processes in state statutes.
Virginia (https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacodefull/title24.2/chapter2/article7/) has a process that is similar to recall, but it is not listed here as a recall state because its process, while requiring citizen petitions, calls for a recall trial rather than an election (Va. Code Ann. §24.2-233 – 24.2.238). In Virginia, after a petition containing the required number of signatures is verified, a circuit court decides whether a Virginia official will be removed from office. In the recall states, the voters decide in an election. Currently, only these 19 states allow recall elections of statewide elected officials, but other states have considered establishing recall procedures. For state legislative action on recalls and other election topics, reference NCSL’s state elections legislation database (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/state-election-legislation-database) and the archived database (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/state-elections-legislation-archived-database), which has legislation from 2011 to 2024.

History
History and Use of the Recall in the U.S.
The recall device began in the United States in a municipality-Los Angeles-in 1903. Michigan and Oregon, in 1908, were the first states to adopt recall procedures for state officials. Illinois became the most recent state to adopt recall procedures for state officials when voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2010 to allow recall of the governor. Before that, Minnesota (1996) and New Jersey (1993) were the most recent.
Historically, recall attempts at the state level have been largely unsuccessful. The recall is used much more often, and with more success, at the local level.
Many attempts have been made to recall governors throughout U.S. history, but only four have gathered enough petition signatures to trigger recall elections. In 2021, California Gov. Gavin Newsom survived a recall election. In 2012, Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker survived a recall election. In 2003, California voters successfully recalled Gov. Gray Davis, and in North Dakota in 1921, voters successfully recalled not only Gov. Lynn J. Frazier, but also the attorney general and the commissioner of agriculture. In 1988, Arizona voters submitted enough signatures to trigger a recall election for Gov. Evan Mecham, but he was impeached by the state's House of Representatives before the scheduled recall election.
Recall efforts against state legislators are more common, but still unusual. Recall attempts against legislators have gathered enough signatures to trigger an election just 40 times. (Many more recall efforts are started and never make it to the election stage.) Eleven of those occurred in a single year, 2011. Forty-three percent of all legislative recall elections that have ever occurred were held between 2011 and 2013. However, only eight of those 17 elections succeeded in unseating a legislator. Overall, 53% of legislative recall elections have succeeded in unseating a legislator. Additionally, two legislators resigned after petitions with sufficient signatures to force recall elections against them were submitted.

The following is a list of every recall election of a state legislator throughout U.S. history. The fact that these elections occurred means that, in each of the following cases, enough signatures were gathered on petitions to trigger a recall election. Pros and Cons
Supporters of the recall process believe it provides a way for citizens to exercise control over elected officials who fail to represent their constituents' best interests, or who are unresponsive or incompetent. This view maintains that an elected representative is an agent or a servant of their constituents, not their master.
Opponents argue that recalls can lead to an excess of democracy: That the threat of a recall election lessens the independence of elected officials; undermines the principle of electing good officials and giving them a chance to govern; and can be abused by well-financed special interest groups and give them undue influence over the political process.
Process
How the Recall Process Works
The recall process varies in its details from one state to another, but in general, recall campaigns follow these steps:
File an application to circulate a recall petition (some states allow petitions only if they contain certain grounds for recall (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Grounds)).

Introduction
In the 19 states that allow state recall elections, citizens can attempt to remove an elected official from office. Typically, the recall process consists of gathering a certain number of signatures on a petition in a certain amount of time. Beyond this, details of the recall process vary by state. This page explains these processes and provides a list of each state's laws governing the recall of state officials.
Overview
Recall is a procedure that allows citizens to remove and replace a public official before the official’s term of office ends. Historically, recall has been used most frequently at the local level. By some estimates, three-fourths of recall elections are at the city council or school board level. This webpage, however, focuses on the recall only as it applies to state officials.
Recall differs from another method for removing officials from office—impeachment (https://www.ncsl.org/about-state-legislatures/separation-of-powers-impeachment)—in that it is a political device while impeachment is a legal process. History
History and Use of the Recall in the U.S.
The recall device began in the United States in a municipality-Los Angeles-in 1903. Michigan and Oregon, in 1908, were the first states to adopt recall procedures for state officials. Illinois became the most recent state to adopt recall procedures for state officials when voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2010 to allow recall of the governor. Before that, Minnesota (1996) and New Jersey (1993) were the most recent.
Historically, recall attempts at the state level have been largely unsuccessful. The recall is used much more often, and with more success, at the local level.
Many attempts have been made to recall governors throughout U.S. history, but only four have gathered enough petition signatures to trigger recall elections. In 2021, California Gov. Gavin Newsom survived a recall election. In 2012, Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker survived a recall election. In 2003, California voters successfully recalled Gov. Gray Davis, and in North Dakota in 1921, voters successfully recalled not only Gov. Lynn J. Frazier, but also the attorney general and the commissioner of agriculture. In 1988, Arizona voters submitted enough signatures to trigger a recall election for Gov. Evan Mecham, but he was impeached by the state's House of Representatives before the scheduled recall election.
Recall efforts against state legislators are more common, but still unusual. Recall attempts against legislators have gathered enough signatures to trigger an election just 40 times. (Many more recall efforts are started and never make it to the election stage.) Eleven of those occurred in a single year, 2011. Forty-three percent of all legislative recall elections that have ever occurred were held between 2011 and 2013. However, only eight of those 17 elections succeeded in unseating a legislator. Overall, 53% of legislative recall elections have succeeded in unseating a legislator. Additionally, two legislators resigned after petitions with sufficient signatures to force recall elections against them were submitted.

Pros and Cons
Supporters of the recall process believe it provides a way for citizens to exercise control over elected officials who fail to represent their constituents' best interests, or who are unresponsive or incompetent. This view maintains that an elected representative is an agent or a servant of their constituents, not their master.
Opponents argue that recalls can lead to an excess of democracy: That the threat of a recall election lessens the independence of elected officials; undermines the principle of electing good officials and giving them a chance to govern; and can be abused by well-financed special interest groups and give them undue influence over the political process.

Pros and Cons
Supporters of the recall process believe it provides a way for citizens to exercise control over elected officials who fail to represent their constituents' best interests, or who are unresponsive or incompetent. This view maintains that an elected representative is an agent or a servant of their constituents, not their master.
Opponents argue that recalls can lead to an excess of democracy: That the threat of a recall election lessens the independence of elected officials; undermines the principle of electing good officials and giving them a chance to govern; and can be abused by well-financed special interest groups and give them undue influence over the political process.
Process
How the Recall Process Works
The recall process varies in its details from one state to another, but in general, recall campaigns follow these steps:
File an application to circulate a recall petition (some states allow petitions only if they contain certain grounds for recall (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Grounds)).
Circulate a recall petition and gather a specified number of signatures in a specified period of time (view the detailed petitioning requirements (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Petition)).
Submit petitions to election officials for verification of signatures.
If enough valid signatures are presented, hold a recall election (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Election).

In most of the recall states, any registered voter can begin a recall campaign for any reason. The language in Michigan's constitution is typical of most states: “The sufficiency of any statement of reasons or grounds ... shall be a political rather than a judicial question.” (Mich. Const. Art. II §8) Indeed, recall campaigns are often politically motivated. For example, in 2011, Republican senators in Wisconsin faced recalls for supporting the governor's effort to reduce the influence of public employee unions, and in Arizona, a senator faced recall for sponsoring a controversial immigration bill.

Alaska: Lack of fitness, incompetence, neglect of duties or corruption (Alaska Stat. §15.45.510)
Georgia: Act of malfeasance or misconduct while in office; violation of oath of office; failure to perform duties prescribed by law; willfully misused, converted, or misappropriated, without authority, public property or public funds entrusted to or associated with the elective office to which the official has been elected or appointed. Discretionary performance of a lawful act or a prescribed duty shall not constitute a ground for recall of an elected public official. (Ga. Code §21-4-3(7) and 21-4-4(c))
Kansas: Conviction for a felony, misconduct in office or failure to perform duties prescribed by law. Misconduct in office means a violation of law by the officer that impacts the officer’s ability to perform the official duties of the office. No recall submitted to the voters shall be held void because of the insufficiency of the grounds, application, or petition by which the submission was procured. (Kan. Stat. Ann. §25-4302)
Minnesota: Serious malfeasance or nonfeasance during the term of office in the performance of the duties of the office or conviction during the term of office of a serious crime (Minn. Const. Art. VIII, §6).
Montana : Physical or mental lack of fitness, incompetence, violation of oath of office, official misconduct, conviction of certain felony offenses (enumerated in Title 45). No person may be recalled for performing a mandatory duty of the office he holds or for not performing any act that, if performed, would subject him to prosecution for official misconduct. (Mont. Code Ann. §2-16-603)
Rhode Island: Authorized in the case of a general officer who has been indicted or informed against for a felony, convicted of a misdemeanor or against whom a finding of probable cause of violation of the code of ethics has been made by the ethics commission. (R.I. Const. Art. IV, §1)
Virginia: Neglect of duty, misuse of office, or incompetence in the performance of duties when that neglect of duty, misuse of office, or incompetence in the performance of duties has a material adverse effect upon the conduct of the office, or upon conviction of a drug-related misdemeanor or a misdemeanor involving a "hate crime." (Va. Code Ann. §24.2-233)
Washington: Commission of some act or acts of malfeasance or misfeasance while in office, or who has violation of oath of office. (Wash. Const. Art. I §33)

content.thinking:
I've found that California and Colorado are the only two states that bar the officeholder from running on the replacement ballot, according to a 2021 NCSL hearing presentation. I'm now checking how the other states handle the recalled official's name on the replacement ballot.

Many other states let the recalled official run again on the replacement ballot, with Arizona, Nevada, and Wisconsin adding them automatically. That makes California's prohibition look unusual, which weakens the SF Chronicle's claim that the provision is unnecessary.

Prop 5's candidacy change turns out to be the mainstream approach, so California's ban is the outlier rather than the restoration. That undercuts the Chronicle's "bizarre flaw" framing, since only California and Colorado bar the recalled official from the replacement ballot.

The remaining states that hold separate special elections, like Georgia and New Jersey, probably don't bar the recalled official either, so Prop 5's candidacy change looks like the national norm and California's ban is the outlier. The NCSL timeline for legislative vacancy special elections also seems to match Prop 5's roughly four-month window, which would fit the current vacancy process.

Now I'm sorting out how the states that do run separate special elections fit in, along with the two-question versus single-question recall setups.

The NCSL breakdown splits states into groups: seven hold recall and replacement votes simultaneously, including California, while the rest run them as separate steps. That means Prop 5 would shift California toward the separate-election majority, which lines up with the Chronicle's point.

Among the states that hold recall and replacement votes separately, the candidacy ban doesn't appear to be common, so the prohibition looks like California's outlier rather than the norm. Prop 5 would remove it and bring California in line with most other states.

The recalled-official ban looks like California's own quirk rather than a national norm, and that undercuts the Chronicle's point about the replacement ballot. Prop 5's other main choices also track common practice, such as separate replacement votes and succession for vacancies. The 2018 plurality winner at 33.8% is a real flaw, and the measure's majority requirement addresses it, so I'm leaning toward yes.

I'm weighing the "No" side's strongest points: voter choice and direct democracy, partisan optics, the cost of legislative recalls, appointment power, and lieutenant governor succession. The public skepticism and the editorial board majority against it are signals I'll weigh too. Given the national-norm evidence, I'm now leaning toward yes.

I'm going to check the NCSL recall page directly to confirm which states hold recall and replacement votes together and which run them separately, and whether the recalled official can appear on the replacement ballot in the separate-election states. I also want to double-check Colorado's rule and whether California really stands out.

Introduction

Overview
Recall is a procedure that allows citizens to remove and replace a public official before the official’s term of office ends. Historically, recall has been used most frequently at the local level. For example, under this Michigan law a voter could initiate a recall against a legislator on the political grounds that the legislator voted against an issue the voter supports. As long as that allegation is stated clearly and factually, it would presumably meet this new criterion.
Circulating a Recall Petition
The recall process is similar to the ballot initiative process in that it requires the submission of citizen petitions. The number of signatures necessary to trigger a recall election, however, is often significantly higher than the number required for ballot initiatives. The required number of signatures is generally equal to a percentage of the vote in the last election for the office in question, although some states base the formula on the number of eligible voters or other numbers. These requirements are listed in the table below.
In many states that allow recalls, there are restrictions on when in an officer’s term a recall petition is permissible. For instance, in Kansas, “no application for the recall of a state officer may be filed during the first 120 days or last 200 days of the term” of the state officer. In Colorado and Michigan, recall petitions cannot be filed during the first or last six months of the term.

The Recall Election
Recalls vary based on how the successor is selected:
Seven states hold recall elections simultaneously with election for a successor for most offices: Arizona, California, Colorado, Michigan, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin.
In five states, a recall election is followed by a separate special election for a successor for most state offices: Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Minnesota and Rhode Island (state legislature only).
In eight states, a successor is appointed to fill a vacancy created by a recall election: Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island (offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer) and Washington.
In some instances, filling vacancies created by recalls differs by office. Ten states—Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island and Washington— fill most state-level recall vacancies through special elections or appointment, but the office of governor is filled by the line of succession. Rhode Island uses both the special election and appointment methods, depending on the office. State legislative recall elections are followed by a separate special election for a successor. For the offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer, recall vacancies are filled by appointment.

In five states, a recall election is followed by a separate special election for a successor for most state offices: Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Minnesota and Rhode Island (state legislature only).
In eight states, a successor is appointed to fill a vacancy created by a recall election: Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island (offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer) and Washington.
In some instances, filling vacancies created by recalls differs by office. Ten states—Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island and Washington— fill most state-level recall vacancies through special elections or appointment, but the office of governor is filled by the line of succession. Rhode Island uses both the special election and appointment methods, depending on the office. State legislative recall elections are followed by a separate special election for a successor. For the offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer, recall vacancies are filled by appointment.
Below is a chart detailing how recall elections are conducted and how a vacancy created by a recall election is filled for state offices. This chart does not cover how judicial vacancies are filled in states where judicial officers may be recalled.

Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Election of State Officials. The State Constitution establishes legislative, executive, and judicial state offices. Some state officials represent parts of the state, known as districts. Other state officials, like the Governor or Attorney General, represent the entire state. Voters elect people to represent them in state offices for set terms. For example, a state Assembly Member is elected to a two-year term and the Governor is elected to a four-year term. To run for a state office, candidates must submit specific nomination documents before the election. State law sets when this “nomination period” occurs.
Recall of State Officials. The State Constitution allows voters to remove state officials from office before their term ends through a recall. A recall is an election in which voters are asked whether to remove an official from office. To qualify a recall for the ballot, supporters of the recall must collect a certain number of signatures from the official’s district (or statewide for statewide offices). Since 1913, 11 state recall efforts have qualified for the ballot (nine legislators and two Governors) and six have resulted in an official’s removal from office (five legislators and one Governor).
Two Questions in Recall Elections. In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office. The number of candidates appearing in the second question varies. For example, there were 135 candidates in the 2003 Governor recall election and 46 candidates in the 2021 Governor recall election. If a state official is recalled, the person who receives the most votes in the second question assumes the office.
Vacant State Offices. State officials may leave office before the end of their term for reasons other than a recall. For example, they may die or resign. When this happens, the office becomes vacant. The process to fill a vacant office varies by office. Typically, a vacant seat in the Assembly or Senate is filled through a special election called by the Governor. The Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor when there is a vacancy in the office of the Governor. Vacancies in other executive offices (for example, the Lieutenant Governor or Attorney General) and the Supreme Court and Courts of Appeal are filled by appointments by the Governor.
Frequency of Elections. Statewide elections in California are scheduled every two years. In scheduled election years, a primary election is held in either March or June, depending on the year, and a general election is held in November. In addition to scheduled elections, the state and local governments may call special elections to address specific issues. For example, the Governor may call a special election to fill a vacant Assembly seat.
Elections Administration in California. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have election-related workload. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
Paying for State Recall Elections. State law requires the California Department of Finance to work with state and local elections officials to estimate the cost of a recall election for a state office. The department is required to send the estimate to the Legislature. The Legislature reviews the estimate and may provide funding for the election. Any remaining costs are paid by the Secretary of State’s and counties’ budgets.
PROPOSAL
As described below, Proposition 5 changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.
Removes Second Question From Recall Elections. Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election. This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices. If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant. Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office. In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election. The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).
Creates Separate Process for Filling the Office of the Governor. The process for filling the office of the Governor depends on when the recall occurs. If the Governor is recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, Proposition 5 says that the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election. If the Governor is recalled later in the term, the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor for the rest of the term.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Fiscal Effects Depend on Frequency of Recalls and the Offices Recalled. Whether there would be costs or savings compared with today depends on the frequency of future recalls and the offices recalled. A recall of a statewide office (for example, Lieutenant Governor) would affect state elections officials and local elections officials in all 58 counties. A recall of a district-based office (for example, a state Senator or Assembly Member) would only affect state elections officials and local elections officials in those districts.
Potential Costs. Proposition 5 could result in higher costs associated with future recall elections if a special election is necessary to fill the vacant office after a recall. For example, a legislative office made vacant after a recall typically would be filled through a special election. If that special election could not be consolidated with a scheduled election, elections officials would need to run a standalone special election. The cost to state and local elections officials to administer such a special election could be millions of dollars per election.
Potential Savings. Proposition 5 could result in lower costs by removing the second question from the ballot. These savings would occur when a Governor is recalled in the latter part of the term and for other offices where vacancies are filled by appointment. There would be savings because ballots and voting materials would no longer include information about replacement candidates. The amount of savings would depend on how many candidates there would have been on the ballot if the second question remained but could be millions of dollars per election.
Net Effect Depends on Circumstances of Future Recall Efforts. The net fiscal effect is unknown because it depends on future recall elections. Proposition 5 could lead to savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars to administer recall elections. How these savings or costs would be shared by state and county governments would depend on future decisions by the Legislature. This net fiscal effect represents less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
California’s recall process should protect our democracy by allowing for the removal of an elected official who is corrupt or abusing their power. It should never be used as a tactic to ‘redo’ an election as a political or partisan scheme. Proposition 5 will restore the recall to its original purpose by making it fair, democratic, and accountable to the will of the majority.
Under current law, a statewide recall ballot asks voters two questions in sequence:
(1) Should the official be recalled? (2) If so, who should replace them?
By being connected, these two questions create a dangerous loophole. An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election. This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this play out in the 2021 gubernatorial recall. Voters rejected it decisively. The recall lost by nearly the same number of votes that the Governor won the regular election with. But California taxpayers were forced to spend more than $200 million on an election whose outcome simply reconfirmed what voters had already decided. Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money. And had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with support from only about 28% of all recall voters.
Proposition 5 makes a single, commonsense change: it removes the second question from the recall ballot .
Under Prop. 5, in a state-level recall, voters would decide one very simple and important question: whether an officeholder should be removed. If a majority votes yes, that office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor and if the recall occurs early enough, voters would elect a replacement at the next statewide election; other statewide officers would be filled by appointment under existing rules; legislative seats by special election. No shortcuts, no loopholes, and no replacement candidate winning office without majority voter support.
In most states with recalls, vacancies are already filled by succession or a separate election, not a same-day replacement contest.
By eliminating the second question, Proposition 5 removes the incentive and ability to weaponize recalls as a shortcut for partisan advantage. Recalls could not be gamed to overturn the results of regular elections or install candidates who couldn’t win under normal conditions.
The framers of our recall process intended to safeguard voters against corrupt and unaccountable officials, not to provide a weapon for political operators to undo election results they don’t like. Proposition 5 preserves the recall as a tool for accountability while preventing it from being used to sidestep regular elections and majority rule.
Vote YES on Proposition 5 to protect majority rule, defend taxpayers, and restore California’s recall process back to the voters it was designed to serve.
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Darius L. Kemp , MPA, Executive Director
California Common Cause
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
California Fair Political Practices Commission
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
Disregard the mental gymnastics the other side is doing here to tie us in knots and try to make sense of the truly nonsensical.
They say Proposition 5 “protects democracy.” It does the opposite-it erodes one of the fundamental elements of our recall process: to choose who replaces the recalled politician.
That’s not protecting democracy-that’s protecting political elites.
They call California’s system a “dangerous loophole.” It’s worked for 100 years, ousting politicians who abuse their office and replacing them with whoever the voters decide will do better.
Proposition 5 would create a loophole, not close one. The other side is gaslighting you. They think you won’t notice. Don’t be fooled.
If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he raised taxes after breaking campaign promises.
Now, he wants to burn it down on his way out the door-making future recalls less effective and keeping politicians like him less accountable.
If you traded in your car, would you want to know what you were getting in return-or would you be happy to sign it away and let the salesman stick you in a jalopy of their choosing after you’ve already committed? That’s what Proposition 5 asks you to do.
Our recall system will continue to work just fine, if we don’t let political elites with sour grapes tinker with it to their benefit.
Vote NO!
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 will take away your voice and erode your ability to remove and replace failed or corrupt politicians from office.
California politicians already have too much power. Proposition 5 gives them even more-and it does it by taking power away from you, the voters.
For over 100 years, California’s recall process has given us the ability to remove elected officials who abuse their office, break promises or fail to do the job they were elected to do. And, when that happens, the current process allows you-not politicians-to choose who replaces them.
Proposition 5 changes that system forever and takes power away from the people.
Today, a recall election asks two simple questions: Should the elected official be removed from office? If so, who should replace them? That means Californians can remove a failed politician and immediately choose someone new to take their place.
Proposition 5 keeps the first part but eliminates your ability to vote for a replacement.
Instead, Sacramento political insiders would decide what happens next. In many cases, politicians themselves-not voters-would choose who fills the vacancy, essentially allowing them to appoint another one of their friends or political allies to replace the one you just ousted.
In other cases, rather than an immediate replacement, the seat would sit vacant until another costly election-funded by you, the taxpayer-was scheduled months later. And here’s the kicker; that failed politician you just ran out the door for failure or corruption, they'd be allowed to run in that next election to regain control of the seat they just lost.
In either case, your vote matters less, and the political establishment gains more control.
Californians deserve the right to remove an elected official-and to choose who comes next. Proposition 5 takes away half of that right, and that’s wrong.
Supporters claim this measure improves democracy. It doesn’t. Democracy means voters-not Sacramento politicians-get to choose their leaders, when to give them the boot and who to replace them with. Proposition 5 undermines that fundamental concept.
Ask yourself: if you vote to remove a governor or another statewide elected official, shouldn’t you also decide who replaces them?
The answer is clear.
It’s also worth wondering why this measure is on the ballot in the first place. Why fix a system that isn’t broken and has been working just fine for over a century?
Well, the author of this proposal himself was recalled by California voters when he voted to raise gas taxes after promising not to. Instead of respecting the will of the people, he now wants to rewrite the rules and protect politicians like him from any meaningful accountability. California’s recall belongs to the people-not politicians. Protect your voice. Protect your vote. Protect your right to hold elected officials accountable.
Vote NO on Proposition 5.
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 5
Don’t be misled. Proposition 5 preserves your power to recall an official by majority vote while closing the loophole that allows a replacement candidate to take office with a small fraction of the vote.
Under current law, voters decide whether to remove an official by majority vote, but the replacement can win with far less than a majority. In 2021, a replacement candidate could have become Governor with support from 28% of recall voters. That is not majority rule.
Opponents want you to believe Proposition 5 takes away your right to choose. It does not. The real question is whether someone should become Governor with support from only a small fraction of California voters.
Proposition 5 preserves the recall while separating the decision to remove an officeholder from the decision about who should serve next. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor-elected statewide by California voters-provides continuity of government until voters choose the next Governor through a regular election. Voters will still choose their elected officials. But candidates seeking statewide office should earn that office in a regular election based on their qualifications, record, and plans for California, not use a recall as a shortcut to power.
A recall should decide whether an officeholder remains in office. Choosing who governs should happen in a regular election, where candidates earn the support of California voters. Proposition 5 protects the recall, respects majority rule, and ensures candidates run on their own merits. Vote YES on Proposition 5.
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Darius L. Kemp , MPA, Executive Director
California Common Cause

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Under current law, voters decide at the same election whether (1) to recall a state officer, and (2) who will replace that officer if recalled.
Under this measure:
if the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor for the remainder of the term or until a successor is elected;
for all other recalled officers, the office will remain vacant until filled by a subsequent special election or appointment as specified in existing law; and
a recalled officer may be a candidate in a special election to fill the office.

Under current law, a California recall election asks voters two questions: should the elected official be removed?
And who should replace them?
Under the current system, if the recall is approved, the candidate who receives the most votes on the second question is named the replacement.
Proposition 5 would change this process by eliminating the replacement question, so voters would decide only whether an elected official should be recalled.
If Prop.
5 passes, separate special elections would replace a recalled assemblymember or state senator, and the governor would appoint someone if a statewide official is recalled.
If a governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would serve as the replacement.
A 'yes' vote on Prop.
5 removes the replacement question from recall ballots, and vacancies would be filled by special election or appointment.
A 'no' vote keeps the current system, where voters choose a replacement on the same ballot.
...
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election.
This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment.
