Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.

We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Newson in 2021, which cost California taxpayers more than $200 million dollars in the midst of an unprecedented public health emergency where those funds were desperately needed for other purposes. Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections. Voters get their say with Prop. 5
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)

Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat.
She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.”
A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms.
If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins.
“I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said.
California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election.
The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections.
However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions.
The “weak gazelle”
Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman.
In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 27 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes.
Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax.
“We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.”
Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes.
In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax.
Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate.
In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy.
“If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said.
But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911.
In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.”
Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill.
“I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.”
Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5.
Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change.
How would it work?
If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election.
If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election.
If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change.
“The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said.
He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections.
However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort.
“It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.”
A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.”
Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions.

I'm noting that the San Francisco Chronicle recommends voting no on Prop 5, and its editorial headline says the measure has a flaw so odd that its own author dislikes it. The paper's core argument is that lawmakers' failure to offer a simple, clean reform is reason enough to reject it. I'm now looking at the specific provision the editorial objects to.

I'm now checking whether the Chronicle has the constitutional provision right, since the measure would overturn a ban on recalled officials running in the special election. I want to confirm the exact wording of that ban in Article II, Section 15 against the proposition text before going further.

Now I'm reading the CalMatters piece on the measure: Democratic lawmakers placed it on the ballot in 2024 with support from good-government groups, and Republicans opposed it. It was a response to the 2021 attempt to recall Governor Newsom, and as of early October the campaigns had raised almost no money.

I'm checking the CalMatters details on the mechanics: if Prop 5 passes, a governor's recall would trigger a special election within about four months, and the ousted official could run in it. I'm also noting that Newman was recalled in 2018 and won back his seat in 2020, which the opponents' framing leaves out.

Now I'm pulling the rest of the CalMatters details: DeMaio argues that the gap in representation could discourage voters from approving a recall, and that extra special elections would roughly double the roughly $200 million the 2021 recall cost. Nalder, a Sacramento State political scientist, thinks the change would mean fewer recalls overall, and that Democrats back it because they win more of the races. The PPIC September survey has 59% of likely voters leaning no, 35% yes, and 5% undecided.

I'm checking whether George Skelton, the LA Times columnist who recommended Yes, speaks for the paper's editorial board or only for himself.

I'm planning to pull the full Mercury News/East Bay Times Q&A with the Yes campaign, the No campaign's Q&A, and the CalMatters voter guide page for Prop 5, plus the LAO analysis to check how the recalled official's eligibility is described.

I'm going to check the measure's full text and the LAO analysis for the Chronicle's constitutional claim. I also want to see how the other major papers and the parties have lined up on Prop 5.

fice. For other elected officials, replacements would be filled in the normal order, just as if they had left office for some other reason, with no new costs associated directly with this change.
Isn’t ranked choice voting a better solution — since it lets voters immediately elect a majority-backed replacement?
It’s a reasonable idea, but it would require every California county to adopt new voting systems, ballot designs and tabulation processes for a scenario, a statewide recall, that arises only a handful of times a decade. Prop. 5 doesn’t hand anyone new power: For governor, the lieutenant governor, already elected statewide, fills the seat temporarily or for the remainder of the term, and where a special election is required, it’s decided by majority with a runoff. That’s a narrower, immediately workable fix to the specific plurality loophole. RCV is worthy of its own debate, especially in light of recent discussions about abandoning the top-two system, but it isn’t on this ballot, and it isn’t a substitute for closing the gap Prop. 5 targets now.
What is the biggest misconception about this proposition?
That the lieutenant governor automatically becomes governor for the rest of the term in every recall. That’s only true in the back half of a term, or once the filing deadline for the next statewide race has passed. Earlier in a term, voters still elect the permanent successor directly, by majority, in a special election. The other misconception is that this change would somehow take power away from voters generally. It won’t. Voters can still decide whether to recall someone, and, where a recall vote is triggered, the replacement process would insulate this important democratic right from partisan distortion and destructive political gamesmanship.
What are we missing? What didn’t we ask?
The world, and especially politics, have changed a great deal since the adoption of the recall, referendum and the initiative more than 100 years ago. Since that time, politics has gotten meaner, more sophisticated and ever-more gameable by effectively the same moneyed interests that the recall was designed to thwart in the Progressive Era. So, it’s worth asking: What happens if this doesn’t pass? The plurality-replacement loophole stays open indefinitely, effectively guaranteeing a repeat of 2021 at some point. The California Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, the State Building and Construction Trades Council and the California Labor Federation all support Prop. 5 with the same objective in mind: ensuring that recall outcomes reflect and serve the true will of the voters. It’s worth asking how this differs for legislative recalls versus the governorship specifically, since the succession mechanics for those seats aren’t identical.

PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

I'm weighing both sides of Prop 5 from the Mercury News/East Bay Times Q&A. The "Yes" side is backed by the state Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and major labor groups. The "No" side's rhetoric is ideological in places, but I'm focusing on its more substantive points: the added cost of a second election, which could force a runoff, and the lieutenant governor appointment question.

Next I'm checking the Mercury News and East Bay Times endorsement guide for their position on Prop 5, and I'll look at the LA Times, Sacramento Bee, and other editorial boards too. I also want the Berkeley IGS and CalMatters voter guides, the PPIC September survey, and the LAO analysis, to verify whether a special election under Prop 5 would go to a runoff.

I'm working out how the special election mechanics apply: a special primary where a majority wins outright, otherwise a special general between the top two. Under that setup, the Yes side's claim that a replacement gets chosen by majority looks largely right for legislative seats. Whether the Governor recall case works the same way is what I still need to check.

I'm now comparing the Yes side's claim about the Governor's successor with what the LAO describes, which says the Lieutenant Governor serves until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election. The Q&A and CalMatters both point to a special election instead, so those sources seem to conflict on this point.

I'm checking the actual text of the measure to settle whether a governor's successor is picked at a special election or at the next regular statewide one, since the LAO, CalMatters, and Berkeley IGS descriptions don't agree. The Q&A's claim that Californians would still choose a permanent successor by majority in an early-term recall depends on that wording.

I'm checking the actual measure text to confirm whether a recalled Governor's successor is chosen at a special election or at the next statewide one, and whether the recalled official can run. I also want the special-election majority and runoff rules and the constitutional section being changed.

I'm going to pull the Prop 5 text and the LAO analysis to settle the successor rules, and check Article II, section 15 on Justia. Then I'll look at the Mercury News/East Bay Times endorsement guide and the LA Times editorial board's position.

I'm now lining up the remaining checks: the Tribune and OC Register endorsements, the California Democratic and Republican Party positions, the PPIC September survey, and Berkeley IGS or Ballotpedia. I also want to see what the 2024 Legislature vote record and any Assembly floor analysis say about why the recalled-official provision was included.

This amendment proposed by Senate Constitutional
Amendment 1 of the 2023–2024 Regular Session
(Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024) expressly
amends the California Constitution by amending
sections thereof; therefore, existing provisions
proposed to be deleted are printed in strikeout type

PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO
ARTICLES II AND V
First—That Section 15 of Article II thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 15. (a) An election to determine whether to
recall an officer and, if appropriate, to elect a successor
shall be called by the Governor and held not less than
60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of
certification of sufficient signatures.
(b) A recall election may be conducted within 180 days
from the date of certification of sufficient signatures in
order that the election may be consolidated with the
next regularly scheduled election occurring wholly or
partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall
election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote
at that next regularly scheduled election equal at least
50 percent of all the voters eligible to vote at the recall
election.
(c) If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the
officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the
candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The
officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any
candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d)
of Section 16 of Article VI. and the office shall be
vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with
this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer
who was the subject of the recall election shall not be
appointed to fill the vacancy in that office.

Second—That Section 17 of Article II thereof is
amended to read:
SEC. 17. If recall of the Governor or Secretary of
State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be
performed by the Lieutenant Governor Secretary of
State or Controller, respectively. If recalls of the
Governor and Secretary of State are initiated at the
same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be
performed by the Controller.
Third—That Section 10 of Article V thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 10. (a) The Lieutenant Governor shall become
Governor when a vacancy occurs in the office of
Governor.
(b) Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 15 of
Article II, if the Governor is removed from office by
recall, the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor
for the remainder of the unexpired term. If the Governor
is removed from office by recall before the close of the
nomination period for the next statewide election during
the first two years of the Governor’s term, a special
election shall be called to replace the Governor and
shall be consolidated with the statewide primary
election and, if necessary, the subsequent statewide
general election. If a candidate receives a majority of
the votes in the special election that is consolidated
with the statewide primary election, that candidate
shall become Governor for the remainder of the
unexpired term. If no candidate receives a majority of
the votes, the top two vote-getters shall compete in a
special election consolidated with the subsequent
statewide general election, and the winner of that
election shall become Governor for the remainder of the
unexpired term.
(c) The Lieutenant Governor shall act as Governor
during the impeachment, absence from the State, or
other temporary disability of the Governor or of a
Governor-elect who fails to take office.
(d) The Legislature shall provide an order of
precedence after the Lieutenant Governor for
succession to the office of Governor and for the
temporary exercise of the Governor’s functions.
(e) The Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction to
determine all questions arising under this section.
(f) Standing to raise questions of vacancy or temporary
disability is vested exclusively in a body provided by
statute.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 13, 2026 at 8:22 AM PDT | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 11:20 AM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Here are our recommendations, so far, for the most competitive races and significant ballot measures on Bay Area voters’ Nov. 3 ballots. To reach our conclusions, we have interviewed more than 70 candidates for federal, state, county, city and school district offices as well as the leaders of committees supporting and opposing initiatives. Please know that, per company policy, we do not endorse in gubernatorial races; and given editorial resources, we prioritize making endorsements in open-seat, or non-incumbent, races. Bookmark this page to view additional endorsements as they are published between now and election day.
Statewide offices
Lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/10/endorsement-elect-fiona-ma-states-next-lieutenant-governor/)
Success as this state’s No. 2 requires understanding its levers of power. Currently treasurer, Fiona Ma already knows how to leverage them. The next lieutenant governor must be as capable of navigating uncharted waters as the governor whom she or he might need to replace at a moment’s notice. By that standard, Fiona Ma is eminently qualified.
(Our interviews with the two candidates for lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma and Gloria Romero — are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/25/in-their-words-fiona-ma-v-gloria-romero-we-asked-they-answered/).)
Treasurer — Eleni Kounalakis (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/endorsement-elect-eleni-kounalakis-californias-next-treasurer/)
California’s next treasurer should expect to inherit the most financially volatile environment since the Great Recession. The state faces long-running structural shortfalls. Growing federal deficits will likely drive up the state’s borrowing costs. Counties are scrambling to fill gaps in once-federally funded services. Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis’ record in business, politics and diplomacy is public and extensive. There are few blanks to fill in. The challenges awaiting the next treasurer require a tested policy and economic operator. That is Lt. Gov. Kounalakis.
(Our interview with Eleni Kounalakis is here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/in-their-words-kounalakis-caballero-tell-us-why-they-can-manage-californias-162-billion/). Jennifer Hawks would not complete our interview request or provide her resume after repeated requests.)
Insurance commissioner — Ben Allen (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/endorsement-elect-ben-allen-californias-next-insurance-commissioner/)
Bay Area voters must understand: When they choose termed-out Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara’s successor, the viability of homeownership is what’s really on the ballot. The conditions for deadlier and most destructive wildfires keep growing. And there is no end in sight. There is only one candidate who grasps the complexity of this crisis and has the legislative experience to address it. That is Ben Allen.
(Our interviews with insurance commissioner candidates Ben Allen and Jane Kim are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/in-their-words-these-candidates-want-to-control-your-home-insurance-heres-why-and-what-theyll-do/).)
Superintendent of Public Instruction — Richard Barrera (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-elect-richard-barrera-californias-superintendent-of-public-instruction-november-election-california-public-schools-sonja-shaw/)
California schools face a constellation of challenges, including declining enrollment, shrinking budgets and persistent achievement gaps. Richard Barrera is a detail-oriented incrementalist focused on student absenteeism and mental health. His opponent, Sonja Shaw, is a brash culture warrior more interested in girls’ locker rooms than the nitty gritty of school reform. We support Barrera.
(Our interviews with Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/richard-barrera-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/) and here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/sonja-shaw-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/), respectively.)
California ballot measures
Prop. 1 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This initiative puts state taxpayers in debt for 25 years and pumps money into a bloated system. Under the best of circumstances, it would add a tiny fraction of the new housing supply needed all while doing next to nothing to solve the real problem: the inexcusably exorbitant cost of building affordable housing.
Prop. 2 — Yes
California’s budget rules perversely count saving as spending, limiting state Legislators’ capacities to bank windfalls for leaner years. That’s fiscal malpractice written into the Constitution. Proposition 2 would exempt rainy day fund deposits from the Gann Limit, double the fund’s cap and require larger deposits when capital gains revenues surge. A state with volatile tax revenues needs a bigger cushion, not obstacles to saving.
Prop. 3 — Yes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/endorsement-proposition-3-california-ballot-measure-progressive-income-tax/)
California’s richest are doing great. Over the last four decades, while the bottom four-fifths of households have seen their real incomes decline, the top 1% have seen their real incomes grow two and half times. This upper stratum now earns in a week what the middle fifth of Californians make in a year. Proposition 3 asks the Californians truly living the California dream — the highest 2% of earners — to keep paying their fair share while also helping the state avoid painful cuts to services induced by President Trump’s and House Republicans’ deliberately punitive H.R. 1, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Prop. 4 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/19/endorsement-reject-prop-4-dont-let-politicians-raid-public-funds-for-their-campaigns/)
Taxpayer dollars must stay reserved to fix municipal roads and parks, rather than finance elections.
Prop. 5 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/20/endorsement-no-on-prop-5-a-bad-idea-that-protects-the-status-quo-and-silences-independent-minded-challengers/)
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Prop. 37 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This measure looks great on the surface. But all that glitters isn’t gold. It would give builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it would artificially inflate the market by putting borrowed cash into buyers’ hands. Instead of lowering construction costs, this merely helps California home buyers take on more debt in the form of second mortgages.
Prop. 38 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/endorsement-no-on-california-proposition-38-an-8-4-billion-money-grab-immunotherapy-ucla-research-ballot-measure/)
This deceptive ballot measure is an $8.4 billion money grab that would funnel taxpayer funds to a single private medical institute run by a billionaire, who is also the chief backer of the Proposition 38 campaign.
Prop. 39 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/15/endorsement-reject-proposition-39-voter-id-fraud-ballot-measure/)
Our editorial board repeatedly asked the Yes on Proposition 39 campaign for evidence of voter fraud in California, rampant or otherwise, and they deflected, dodged and denied the premise of our questions. In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots (among other restrictive voting rules and audits), it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding and repeatedly debunked claims that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections. This initiative is an expensive solution to a phantom problem. Reject Proposition 39.

The low signature threshold goes untouched, which means the measure is at best a partial fix.

I'm now weighing the editorial positions: the SF Chronicle and Mercury News recommend No, pointing to the recalled official's ability to run again and the loss of voter choice in replacement, while the LWV, Common Cause, and other advocates back Yes. I still need to confirm where the LA Times editorial board actually stands.

I'm weighing the pro case for Prop 5: the plurality replacement rule is the main loophole, and majority rule plus less incentive for partisan recalls, backed by good-government groups and the Secretary of State, carry real weight. I also want to check the 2021 numbers, since the Yes side's claim that the leading replacement had only about 28% of recall voters may be measuring something different from the replacement vote share.

I'm checking Schwarzenegger's 2003 result, where he won about 48.6% of the replacement vote among 135 candidates, which is a large plurality rather than a thin one. That makes me wonder whether plurality winners still tend to have broad support, even though the Yes side frames the replacement share as small.

I'm checking the 2021 replacement numbers against the Yes side's claim that Elder would have won with only about 28% of recall voters, since the share of the replacement vote I half-remember may be a different measure altogether.

Next I'm checking Elder's 2021 replacement share, since the Yes side's 28%-of-recall-voters figure may not match the replacement vote numbers I half-remember. I'll search for the official results to settle it.

I'm planning the next checks: the LAO analysis on the recalled official's candidacy and the special election timeline, the Mercury News and LA Times editorial positions, the other papers' endorsements, the latest PPIC and Berkeley IGS polls, party stances, and the 2021 and 2018 replacement vote shares, starting with Elder's figure.

I'm planning the next searches: fetching the official 2021 and 2003 replacement results to settle Elder's share, plus the Prop 5 fundraising totals and the Mercury News and LA Times editorial positions.

content.text: The measure text confirms the most important detail: it would remove the constitutional bar on a recalled officer running in the replacement election. I'll pull the Mercury News No endorsement and check other editorial boards and the poll.

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

I'm checking whether the measure's own wording creates a problem, since it's a constitutional change and some of its provisions look hard to justify. I'm also weighing how a partisan split and the sponsor's background might shape how voters read it, and whether the ballot title could leave people thinking it only covers statewide offices.

I'm checking the cost side more closely: the measure's savings would be modest, since the election itself is the main expense, and the specific savings depend on whether a replacement contest is held at all. The ballot label also seems to cover only statewide officers, though the amendment reaches legislative recalls too. Next I'm looking at what supporters can point to in favor of the measure.

I'm noting that Prop 5's fix for plurality wins would make replacements for legislative and gubernatorial seats need a majority, which would be a real gain in legitimacy. I'm also weighing whether it cuts the incentive for targeted recalls aimed at installing a preferred candidate with a plurality, as with the Newman recall.

I'm noting that the endorsements from the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, the Secretary of State, and the state party and labor, along with several columnists and the Sacramento Bee's board, all line up on the yes side. The strongest "no" points, the appointment power and the Lieutenant Governor succession, look more like standard vacancy practice than a fresh power grab, though the recalled-official loophole still reads as a flaw.

I'm weighing whether the recalled-official provision really matters: a candidate would still need a majority in a special election, so it's a fresh voter choice, though the optics and possible misuse of recall money still count against it. The main question is whether ending plurality replacements is worth the loss of direct voter choice, and several well-informed editorial boards land on no.

I'm noticing the legislative vote counts don't fit with what I'd read about Republicans opposing the measure, since a 32-8 Senate tally would mean at least a couple of Republicans voted yes. I'll need to check which account is right before I rely on the partisan framing.

I'm checking the Senate tally against the party split, since 32 ayes would need at least two Republicans voting yes, which doesn't match the partisan framing I'd been relying on. I still need to decide whether the appointment power and the recalled-official provision outweigh the gain from ending plurality replacements, and the drafting flaw is the part that leans me toward no.

I'm weighing whether the plurality flaw is serious enough to justify a constitutional change that brings its own problems. The SF Chronicle's view that the replacement question could be fixed on its own gives some support to that, while the Mercury News frames a plurality win as a legitimate expression of voter will.

I'm settling on a leaning toward no: the measure as drafted removes direct voter choice, lets the recalled official run again, and leaves vacancy gaps for legislative seats, while the plurality problem could be fixed more cleanly on its own. I'm also noting that the polling has tightened, though it still leans against the measure.

I'm weighing the case for yes: the plurality problem is a real flaw that Prop 5 targets directly, and the other concerns look more like standard vacancy practice than a new power grab. I'm now picturing a concrete recall scenario to test whether replacement by plurality actually produces a worse outcome than the measure would.

I'm working through a recall scenario now: if a state senator is recalled, the current rule would seat whoever leads the replacement race, possibly with only about a quarter of the vote. I'm weighing that against Prop 5's appointment route, where a Democratic governor would fill the seat, which avoids a minority win but drops voter choice altogether.

I'm now testing a recall of a governor early in the term: under current law a plurality could seat almost anyone, while under Prop 5 the lieutenant governor would serve until a majority-decided special election, though that means months under an acting official.

I'm working through the governor case now: a recall late in the term would hand the remaining years to the lieutenant governor, who is elected statewide but never ran for that seat. That's the part of Prop 5 that feels least democratic, though it's an elected official rather than an unknown plurality winner, so it's a close call on legitimacy.

I'm weighing the case for and against: the measure's majority-rule replacement would be a real gain, with costs in appointments, legislative gaps, and the recalled-official candidacy flaw. The public polls skew skeptical, and party cues may drive many voters, but on the merits this looks like a close call that could reasonably go either way.

I'm weighing the arguments against Prop 5 on their merits: the Mercury News critiques read more like rhetoric and speculation, while the Chronicle's point about the recalled official's candidacy is a concrete drafting flaw I can point to. I'm also considering whether the appointment and succession concerns hold up once I compare them against how current recall replacements actually work.

I'm reading through the arguments the League of Women Voters and Common Cause make for the yes side, and the LAO's analysis, which treats the fiscal effect as unknown and stays neutral on policy. The PPIC poll still has most likely voters leaning no, and I want to check the Sacramento Bee's reasons for backing yes before I put much weight on it.

I'm considering the recall scenarios more concretely now: a recalled legislator who runs again is a limited but real concern, since most recall targets are unpopular and rarely return. For statewide officers, the governor's appointee would serve only until the next general election, so the power-grab worry looks modest, though the incumbency edge still deserves a look.

I'm weighing the downsides of Prop 5 as moderate: the legislative special election gap and cost, and the lieutenant governor's takeover, both look limited. On the other side, majority-chosen replacements are a real gain, so I'm inclined to lean toward yes.

I'm checking the Mercury News's claim that Bustamante would have been the favorite in a later election, which would make Prop 5 produce a different outcome than the immediate replacement vote did. The current process at least gave voters a direct choice, and Prop 5 would take that away.

I'm weighing the case that the measure is a close call that depends on values, though the user wants a yes or no. Several policy voices I'm tracking, including the elections office, the League of Women Voters, and Common Cause, back Prop 5, while the newspapers that oppose it are the ones I'd need to weigh against that.

I'm weighing the case that a no vote is the safer default, since the plurality loophole hasn't yet produced a clearly bad recall outcome and Prop 5 brings new mechanisms like the lieutenant governor succession, appointments, and short special-election gaps that haven't been tested.

I'm weighing the expected value here: a statewide recall in the next decade seems fairly unlikely, so Prop 5's changes would only matter in rare cases. Either choice mostly affects an uncommon scenario, which makes the "when in doubt, don't change the constitution" argument for No feel reasonable. Still, the plurality flaw is real, and the question is whether fixing it is worth the new mechanisms it introduces.

I'm now weighing whether Prop 5's fewer-recalls effect is a gain or a loss: supporters see less hyperpartisan churn, while opponents see weaker public power to remove officials, since a replacement gap makes removal less attractive.

I'm leaning toward "no" but it's close to a coin flip, since the accountability cost of Prop 5 (voters hesitating to recall when replacement takes months) is a real downside. I'd like to check more expert analyses, like the Berkeley IGS, Ballotpedia, and the Sacramento Bee's case for yes, before settling on it.

I'm checking the Chronicle and Daily News reasons for opposing, along with the Sacramento Bee's case for yes, and whether any results are already in. If the vote has happened, that changes the question, so I'll look for that first.

I'm going to pull up the CalMatters article from Nov 3 next, since it's the most recent coverage, and see if any results are in yet.

content.text: Editorial boards are mostly against Prop 5, while the Sacramento Bee's owner and several columnists back it. The October PPIC poll also moved toward yes. I'll check the newest CalMatters piece, look for any results, and verify the Sacramento Bee and San Diego Union-Tribune positions.

Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)

This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.
Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time.
Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021.
The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.
Where Prop. 5 came from
In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office.
Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win.
They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections.
Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker.
Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003.

Proposition 5 seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide.
Such elections have been rare in California.
...
If Prop.
5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled.
If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held.
If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor.
Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until a special election was held.
If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.

California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms. Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes. Where Prop. 5 came from In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker. Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003. READ NEXT Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections. Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?

By Kate Wolffe, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.

Proposition 5 would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. 

Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. 

The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it, while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.

Where Prop. 5 came from

In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. 

Weber and good governance groups argued the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. 

They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. 2026 Election: California Ballot proposition endorsements from our opinion team could help make tough choices
By Teagan Davidge, The Orange County Register
The Tribune Content Agency
October 20, 2026 5:41 PM
Voters have through Nov. 3 to cast their ballots, but election officials are especially encouraging those who vote by mail to do so early. (Photo by Mark Rightmire, Orange County Register/SCNG)
Mark Rightmire
TNS
To help you make decisions about the 14 statewide propositions on California's ballot, our opinion team made recommendations like it does for every election. The process is completely separate from newsroom reporting and journalists.
But the team considers arguments from across the political spectrum while developing its editorial stance. We understand that not everyone will agree with these endorsements – that's the nature of politics.
If you’d rather read impartial articles from our reporters, they covered all 14 propositions in this guide: All 14 propositions before California voters this year, explained (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/07/02/election-2026-all-14-propositions-before-california-voters-this-year-explained/)
We hope it helps you clarify your own reason for choosing how to vote.
Tax-related💲
❌ No on Prop 2, California's rainy day fund: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-no-on-prop-2-california-needs-fiscal-discipline-not-accounting-tricks/)Prop. 2 would double the state budget reserve cap from 10% of General Fund revenues to 20% of General Fund revenues. The General Fund is the state's main spending account.
❌ No on Prop 3, Income tax rates: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/02/endorsement-no-on-proposition-3-temporary-taxes-should-be-temporary/)Prop 3 would extend the state’s highest income tax rates, which are now up to 12% for single filers who earn more than $360,000 per year and other high income groups, past 2031.
❌ No on Prop 40, One-time tax on billionaires: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/)This measure, known as the "Billionaire Tax Act," would enact a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires to raise temporary revenue to address the loss of federal funding to health, nutrition, and education services, largely a result of the 2025 budget reconciliation law known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill."
✅ Yes on Prop 41, Audits and limitations on special taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/21/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-41-and-42-to-limit-taxation-in-california/)Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. It would also require new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit - the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year, therefore blocking Prop 40, the "Billionaire Tax."
✅ Yes on Prop 42, Ban on new personal property taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/21/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-41-and-42-to-limit-taxation-in-california/)Prop 42 is another attempt to block Prop 40, this time by prohibiting new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property. California doesn't currently tax financial assets, and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees).
Government & Election Reform 🏛️
❌ No on Prop 4, Expansion of public campaign financing programs: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)Prop 4 would lift a ban that keeps counties, districts, most cities and the state from giving candidates public funds to run for election if they agree to certain terms. Cities won't automatically offer the program, but they would have that option.
❌ No on Prop 5, Changes to recall elections of state officials: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)This measure would make state recall elections just a yes or no question and remove the "Who should replace them?" query. If the governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would fill the role, and for other state offices, vacancies would be filled according to state law.
✅ Yes on Prop 39, Voter ID for future elections: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/15/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-39/)Prop 39 would change the current protocol by requiring all voters to show ID when voting in person or provide the last four digits of their ID number when voting by mail. Election officials would also be required to report the percentage of county voters whose citizenship has been verified.
✅ Yes on Prop 43, New threshold for passing local taxes: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)Right now, it takes 50% of voters to approve a local tax that appears on a ballot through the signature-gathering process. If Prop. 43 passed, it would raise that threshold to 75% for a new tax, a tax increase or an extension to be implemented.
Housing & Social Infrastructure 🏡
❌ No on Prop 1, Veterans and affordable housing bonds: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/23/endorsement-no-on-prop-1-more-debt-wont-fix-californias-housing-shortage/)This measure would allow the state to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to fund affordable housing efforts.
❌ No on Prop 37, Home loans to middle-income earners: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/)Prop 37 would let the state issue $25 billion in bonds to help middle-income homebuyers afford homes.
❌ No on Prop 38, Immunology and immunotherapy research: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/23/endorsement-no-on-proposition-38-an-8-4-billion-money-grab/)Prop 38 would approve $8.4 billion in bonds toward California nonprofit universities' medical research into treatments that use the body's own immune system to treat disease.
❌ No on Prop 44, Community clinic spending: (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/08/endorsement-no-on-proposition-44-a-cynical-attack-on-community-health-clinics/)Prop 44 would make it so safety-net health clinics must spend 90% of their revenue on providing services to underserved people, rather than on management.
✅ Yes on Prop 45, Changes to CEQA (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/09/endorsement-yes-on-prop-45-to-reform-ceqa/) (California Environmental Quality Act): Prop 45 would speed up California's environmental impact review process for certain projects like housing, transportation and infrastructure by limiting its scope and setting review deadlines for public agencies.
